Our research looks at the Compressed Dark Matter (CDM) model, which involves a baryon number-conserving theory, to examine whether it can explain the recently observed $26.7~\text{GeV}$ invariant mass in the D0 $\gamma\gamma$ spectrum. In order to achieve this, we introduce a new Yukawa interaction between two compressed dark matter fields that enables them to couple with photons. By applying the next-to-leading order precision in the CDM mass, we find that the observed feature can be reproduced when the CDM mass is approximately $50~\text{GeV}$, the coupling constant ranges from $1.3\times10^{-3}$ to $1.4\times10^{-3}$, and the difference in the CDM masses is around $\pm1~\text{GeV}$. We also provide the forecasted bounds that the FASER experiment will likely impose on the CDM scenario with a $50~\text{GeV}$ invariant mass.

Neural networks' training has been compared to a lottery, with multiple winners emerging from our research in *Seelig and Cubeddu, 2021*. We have discovered that fixed architectures of sparse recurrent neural networks are capable of learning a wide range of complex cognitive tasks more efficiently than dynamic neural networks. Despite having limited computational resources, these networks can still achieve exceptional performance, similar to state-of-the-art results for various benchmark datasets. The time it takes to train these networks is proportional to the number of connections between neurons, a significant improvement over current training methods. To illustrate the potential of this type of network, we have applied it to tasks in visual navigation and language understanding, and the results are available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/CUBEDDU/spRN_CogSci.

Researchers classify nilpotent algebras by examining the structure of their socle chain, which leads to the identification of fundamental spaces, and subsequently, a geometric classification of nilpotent algebras based on categorification principles. The 1-categorical structure of nilpotent algebras is fully determined, while the enhanced structure remains incomplete without additional data. Despite this challenge, the established classification proves valuable in the study of representation theory in various settings.

Active galactic nuclei with massive black holes that emit powerful jets are thought to be among the brightest objects in the early universe, potentially surpassing the CMB in brightness at very high redshifts. In a recent study, we explored how the CMB interacts with these jets in the early universe, and discovered that they have a significant impact on the evolution of black holes and their ability to launch relativistic jets. At redshifts above 10, the CMB's radiation pressure equals the pressure of the black hole's accretion disk, and a significant portion of this energy is transferred to the jet fluid, causing it to accelerate. In turn, this jet acceleration leads to a reduction in the black hole's growth rate, and as a result, the black hole's mass increases more slowly than expected, while its spin decreases. Furthermore, the CMB's influence also causes the jet to lose energy to the surrounding interstellar medium, rather than being directed towards the poles of a distant observer's sky, as previously assumed. Instead, the CMB's energy is distributed equally in all directions, resulting in a reduction in the polarisation of the jet. Based on these findings, we adjusted a model of black hole growth to account for the CMB's influence, and discovered that black hole masses are significantly reduced at high redshifts as a result of the CMB's interaction. In turn, this has a significant impact on the distribution of black holes in a given mass range at later

We've discovered that the gravitational field in classical General Relativity lacks a defined Lagrangian. There are multiple obstacles to forming a Lagrangian, including its non-linearity and lack of symmetry, as well as the difficulties posed by holonomies and curvature variability. Despite these challenges, we suggest that the concept of a 'effective Lagrangian' could be applicable on an effective level. An 'effective Lagrangian' would refer to an effective spatial concept that describes the gravitational field's behavior in terms of spatial metrics and their evolution over time. Additionally, we outline an approach to deriving an effective point mass representation of the Lagrangian based on a finite source count. This involves considering the geometric properties of closed surfaces surrounding distant masses in a 4D spacetime.

This study presents advancements to the 3D Shift Invariant Feature and corresponding matching algorithm, also incorporating SP-Symmetry for constructing image representations. A method for generating local templates from a model's volume is outlined, leveraging the robust features derived from 3D SIFT. An efficient scheme for grouping these features into a single signature has been developed, achieving better results according to the measures defined in the Volume2Surface benchmark. Building upon these improvements, this paper contributes Entropy-based SP-Symmetry Weighted Voting, a more comprehensive approach for matching features, increasing the accuracy of volume matching. Notably, our proposed method surpasses the state-of-the-art performance in the Volume2Surface benchmark.

Our target, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, is a well-known double-degenerate binary system exhibiting a 40.5-minute eclipsing period and exhibiting P-EBDI (period-exchanged bright-dim) phenomena. This study aims to undertake detailed photometric and time-resolved spectroscopic examinations of the system to establish its physical characteristics and to determine whether the transferred matter from the white dwarf to the companion star during the 40.5-minute eclipses results in the P-EBDI phenomenon.

Our initial observations revealed a 40.5-minute eclipsing period and detected the white dwarf and companion star's photometric systems to be composed of three and two components respectively. Through the analysis of our multi-band photometry, we were able to determine the system's smaller and larger zero-age main-sequence mass to be 0.095 and 0.26 $M_{\odot}$ respectively, and our time-resolved spectroscopic examinations allowed us to detect no noticeable variations in the helium and helium-absorption features, suggesting that the non-detection of these variations could be attributed to the system's small system velocity amplitude.

We were able to demonstrate that our multi-component multi-band photometry fits the system's data perfectly, and through the application of diverse models, we were able to determine the system's small and large radius to be 0.025 and 0.33 $R_{\odot}$ respectively. This research revisits global aggregation techniques in deep learning with the insight from optimal transport theory. By leveraging the connection between aggregation and optimal transport, we pinpoint the shortfalls of existing methods, primarily the inability to effectively combine diverse sources of information. We address this limitation by developing the first neural network capable of performing well-defined global aggregation tasks without relying on explicit mapping functions. The proposed approach successfully tackles multi-source image aggregation and global feature aggregation within the context of semantic segmentation. The resulting model demonstrates considerable improvements when applied to image aggregation and achieves superior results in Bellagio dataset challenge.

This study reveals distinct host galaxy characteristics for different types of Active Galactic Nuclei, with Type 1 AGN having brighter and larger cores than Type 2 AGN, and also identifies three distinct host galaxy types for Type 1 AGN based on optical and mid-infrared luminosity. A linear relationship between the optical and mid-infrared luminosities of the host galaxy has been established. The distribution of the host galaxy mass was found to be significantly affected by orientation, with higher masses for Type 1 AGN when compared to Type 2 AGN, and found no significant evidence to support a relationship between the black hole mass and AGN type. The influence of inclination angle on host galaxy mass and surface brightness was observed. The study suggests that accretion rate could be the driving force behind the variation in host galaxy properties.
This research paper confirms that a particular solution to the Einstein field equations in 4D space-time, described by a 1-type Gauss metric in 4D space-time, corresponds to a flat rotational plane.

Advances in computer vision have reached new heights thanks to large-scale image datasets and advanced machine learning techniques. Deeper models induced by extensive training on such datasets have led to remarkable accuracy gains. Initially developed for specific tasks, these models can now be leveraged for various applications through transfer learning. However, transferring Inductive models to different tasks may not always be effective if the data distribution changes significantly. As such, Discrimative models, optimized for data with associated task labels, have been explored as transfer learning options. Moreover, Discrimative models pre-trained on depth maps have shown benefits for semantic segmentation by improving feature learning. Conversely, we discovered that certain depth maps are inadequate for top-notch semantic segmentation. As such, we do not recommend using depth maps as a discriminative pre-training option. Instead, we propose a novel dataset, DDT-20K, comprising image sets with associated depth maps, which serves as the basis for our study's evaluations.

We introduce TCube, a novel neural network approach for generating stories about time-series data, focusing on explaining trend changes in financial time-series. Unlike existing methods that require domain-specific knowledge, TCube can translate various time-series trends into understandable stories without excessive training in a specific domain. Our approach involves using a trend detection module to identify shifts in the data and then generates stories with explicitly stated causes and effects, enabling users to easily identify the trend and its explanation. TCube effectively produces stories for real-world financial datasets from various industries, such as stocks and crypto, by incorporating trend analysis. Our experiments demonstrate that TCube's stories accurately represent the data's causal structure and outperform a comparison method in clarity, with a 95% success rate. Our code and pre-trained models are available for download at the URL.

The precision in determining CP violation in beauty mesons has been a major constraint in past particle physics studies. Studies at the LHC have significantly improved our understanding, while remaining data limitations have led to the development of the Belle II experiment, which is expected to significantly enhance our knowledge. This article discusses recent findings from the ATLAS experiment at the LHC, focusing on a few areas: a search for rare occurrences of the decay process $B_s^{0}$ into $J/\psi$ and $\eta^-$, a search for CP violation in certain decay processes involving $B^0_s$ mesons, and a investigation into the occurrence of certain decay processes involving $B^0_s$ mesons that do not conform to the standard model predictions.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze periodical Ising model configurations, extending the existing literature which focused on the unique periodic configurations in the model's external field setting. We demonstrate that, in the absence of an external field, there exists a diverse array of periodical configurations. Specifically, for any given period k, we have established the existence of a distinct periodical Ising model configuration, separately for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic scenarios, which is unique to its corresponding parameter space. Additionally, we have found additional periodical configurations, both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic, for the Ising model on a Cayley tree.

This research addresses the issue of solving a global partial differential equation in its hyperbolic form, with the equation featuring non-convex coefficients that result in an anisotropic hyperbolic equation. The nonlinearity present in this problem is characterized by sublogarithmic growth, with its coefficients bounded below by a positive constant for all times. By developing an energy method that accounts for energy's anisotropic properties, we establish the existence of a single global solution that is continuous over time, effectively resolving a fundamental problem in the geometric theory of hyperbolic equations.

This research introduces Enhanced JWD-ET, a enhanced version of the Short-Term Memory Model, for the task of dividing Japanese written words into their correct components. As a pure neural network model, Enhanced JWD-ET surpasses the performance of its predecessor and a popular competing model, ultimately achieving a notable 91.56% accuracy in word division.

On Stack Overflow, users engage with external links via comments to share useful information, often making the platform's answers more comprehensive. This study aimed to understand the role of these external links in enhancing Stack Overflow content. Through a large-scale examination of the data, we identified key findings. Firstly, external links were found to be associated with high-quality answers on the platform. The data also showed that answers containing these links receive more upvotes, demonstrating their positive impact on answer quality and visibility. Furthermore, users frequently share links to establish answer preconditions, highlighting the importance of such resources in facilitating answer comprehension. About half of the external links on Stack Overflow are still accessible, with users indicating the reason for sharing the link in comments. To improve the data quality, we propose several strategies for Stack Overflow moderators and algorithmic enhancement techniques to effectively manage these links, ultimately facilitating better data collection for research purposes.

One of the long-standing issues in astrophysics is the galaxy variability problem, which has been persistent for 50 years. Researchers face a daunting task of explaining the maintenance of heavy elements in galaxies when light elements predominate the universe's primordial composition. Until now, numerous proposed solutions have failed to substantially address the issue, and many of the established models themselves are unreliable. We examine the underlying mechanisms of 11 possible explanations for galaxy variability, including the variations in the universe's metallicity, star formation processes, the interaction between galaxies, the role of stellar winds and other active galactic nuclei, and the presence of dark matter. We also conduct a thorough evaluation of each model's strengths and weaknesses, discussing their potential applications and observations that could test them. Ultimately, we identify key areas of research that require further investigation to resolve the galaxy variability problem.

Despite widespread consensus on climate change, meaningful discussions are often hindered by conflicting views, data disparities, and comprehension gaps. To enhance climate conversations, we introduce the Climate Data Repository, a comprehensive resource that bridges these obstacles by connecting users with relevant factual information. Implemented across various platforms, including Facebook Groups and Meetup, this resource has demonstrated promising results in fostering productive discussions and promoting collective climate action initiatives. In this research, we evaluate the effectiveness of the Climate Data Repository and examine its potential applications in revitalizing climate dialogue.

Preserving patient anonymity is a top priority when analyzing medical data. One key aspect is to conceal sensitive information in hospital records by hand. Existing automated solutions focused on extracting vital information are still limited by their reliance on specific medical institutions and can only handle a limited number of conditions. This study seeks to resolve this issue by using a medical knowledge base to uncover symptoms not explicitly mentioned in patient notes. We developed EmotionlessME, an emotionless medical event extraction algorithm that combines attention-based neural networks with contrastive learning to identify various symptoms on a larger scale. Our tests showcase significant enhancements over current approaches in three distinct medical datasets. Furthermore, we discovered that our method successfully detects symptoms not explicitly mentioned in patient notes while maintaining accurate extraction of mentioned symptoms.

Deep reinforcement learning has gained significant attention in the field of autonomous driving technology development. The combination of reinforcement learning's potential to guide complex decision-making and deep neural networks' ability to model this complexity effectively has made deep RL a prominent driver of recent advancements in AD. Although significant progress has been achieved, deep RL still faces significant hurdles in overcoming the intricacies of autonomous driving, particularly in the areas of scissor-joint collisions and uneven road surfaces. This article discusses the current state of deep RL in autonomous driving and presents a new approach using a deep RL model based on a race car scenario.

Deep brain-like structures exhibit stable behavior over an extended period, but
their current digital models consume excessive energy. Recent studies have used
spiking neural networks to develop more computationally efficient artificial
inteligence systems. Researchers have explored the potential of leveraging
surrounding circuit mechanisms, such as axon dynamics and synapse plasticity, 
to further optimize these systems and achieve significant reduction in 1) the
number of used synapses, 2) post-stimulation neuron activation, and 3) 
energy consumption while maintaining accurate classification performance. To 
address these challenges, we re-evaluated the design principles of the brain and
developed novel algorithms for training spiking neural networks. Our proposals 
involve the introduction of a local leverage mechanism, the adaptation of the
Bishop curve using a stabilized gradient algorithm, and the application of a
stable leaky Integrate-and-Fire model. Our experiments demonstrate that the
newly proposed models require substantially fewer synapses and post-stimulation
neurons compared to existing solutions, ultimately leading to a notable energy 
savings of approximately 10 times over our previous study. These improved models
can be utilized in edge computing and resource-constrained environments for 
spiking neural network-based AI services.

This research investigates the properties of quark star matter consisting of up, down, and strange quarks under the influence of a spin alignment effect at higher temperatures and in the presence of a strong magnetic field. We have examined how the spin alignment impact, couple with the magnetic field, influences the equation of state, as well as the star's mass and radius across various temperatures. Notably, at higher temperatures, the spin alignment contribution becomes insignificant in the presence of a strong magnetic field, leading to quark star matter behaving like free fermions. We have also analyzed how the spin alignment effect impacts the star's bulk properties in comparison to matter aligned by temperature, as well as in comparison to non-aligned star matter in an alternative model. Importantly, our findings indicate that the spin alignment effect leads to quark star matter consisting of up, down, and strange quarks having a higher radius and lower mass than aligned star matter consisting of up, down, and constituent quarks in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Additionally, our findings show that the spin alignment effect leads to quark star matter consisting of up, down, and strange quarks having a higher radius and lower mass than star matter consisting of up, down, and strange quarks in the Nambu--Gorkov model.

Current Vue.js web applications can leverage the browser's computational power, utilizing parallel JavaScript execution, to enhance performance. We introduce Pando, a lightweight framework empowering developers to tap into the collective computing power of individual volunteers' browsers. Pando facilitates creators in expanding their application's computational capabilities, enabling complex calculations and data-intensive processing. The framework's key features include a unified task distribution system across multiple browsers and a flexible, decentralized processing management system. Furthermore, Pando features a resource monitoring tool, which keeps developers informed about active contributors and their allocated resources. We showcase the functionality of Pando in a demonstration project, demonstrating its potential to make volunteer computing more accessible and user-friendly.

This research examines estimates for nonlinear eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix, defined by a nonlinear equation involving polynomials of the matrix entries. We analyze an estimation method based on a minimal rational interpolation model and investigate its performance in a non-parametric sense. Key factors influencing the estimation error are the degree of the polynomial and a regularization parameter. Notably, this estimation method can also be utilized to study the local characteristics of matrices. Our study demonstrates that this approach provides adaptive results under certain conditions and specifies a critical value for the regularization parameter that achieves optimal results. Additionally, we propose a novel estimation method for nonlinear eigenvectors that achieves optimal results in a non-parametric sense. Our results are supported by numerical simulations, which verify the theoretical findings and highlight the approach's practical applications.

We establish a link between intermediate beta shifts and avaricious beta shifts with a gap. This relationship enables us to derive fresh insights into the nature of these transitions. For instance, we prove that certain avaricious beta shifts with a gap encompass a broad category of beta shifts associated with Markov partitions of hyperbolic conformal maps. Additionally, we demonstrate that an essential aspect of the class of avaricious beta shifts with a gap is that they exhibit ergodic properties.

In this context, we're investigating a specific set of gauge theories, denoted by $SO(N_c)$ with an $SO(N_f)$ global symmetry, to analyze the behavior of these theories as $N_f$ and $N_c$ increase. These theories are known to be similar to $Sp(N_c)$ and $SU(N_c)$ gauge theories with a global $O(N_f)$ symmetry, yet exhibit distinct behavior in certain limits. By considering a lattice regularizations of these theories, we demonstrate the existence of two distinct phases: a confining phase characterized by string-like excitations and a disorder phase with increased degeneracy in the spectrum. Using numerical computations on the lattice, we show that the string tension in the confining phase disappears at a finite temperature, marking a phase transition. This transition represents a manifestation of chiral symmetry disruption. Unlike its $Sp(N_c)$ and $SU(N_c)$ counterparts, this phase transition does not coincide with the onset of confinement, highlighting a complex and possibly anachronistic nature of chiral symmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as Random Forests and Boosted Trees provide strong performance across various domains, but their complex structure makes it difficult to understand their decisions. Research has focused on understanding individual tree models through visualization, but this approach becomes impractical when dealing with the many trees in a Forest. Our proposed method develops a graphical representation to interpret these models, revealing correlations between features and predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments involving real-world datasets, and also examine its applicability to other models such as Neural Networks.

The security requirements of machine learning models have evolved from mere regulatory compliance to a genuine concern for potentially sensitive model owners.  Two emerging technologies have been proposed to address these needs:  Federated Learning, which decentralizes training across numerous clients, and Trusted Execution Environments, which provide secure execution environments.  This paper presents Flatee, an innovative framework that seamlessly integrates these technologies to enable training ML models within a secure execution environment while maintaining client data privacy.  By combining the benefits of both Federised Learning and Trusted Execution Enclaves, Flatee offers a highly secure solution for potential attackers and data-proud owners.  The paper's results demonstrate that Flatee can effectively resist software-based and hardware-based attacks, and it offers a notable performance improvement compared to existing ML training methods.

For demonstrating model-based design and validation, a portable, open-source toolset is described, which successfully implements a industrial-scale robotic application on a low-cost, embedded target hardware. The toolset is composed of PSA-based validation techniques, paired with a lightweight device emulator, and showcases the effectiveness of using automated verification on real hardware. Despite hardware limitations, the toolset achieves practical results for industrial applications.

This research introduces a new technique for automatically generating system call
policies between containerized microservices applications without interrupting service,
using only simple API calls. The method creates an individual policy for each
microservice by observing the system call patterns of a specially prepared testing
environment, comprising of isolated worker functions and an administrative module.
During testing, the administrator interacts with the application via the module, 
while the worker modules generate new variants of their own system call patterns in
response to changes in their requirements without affecting the running application.
A dynamic model is then developed for each service to simulate these variations,
all within a temporary environment separate from the main application. 
The methods for observing, dynamic modeling, and policy learning are explained in
detail, along with a comprehensive evaluation of the approach on a range of real-world
applications, including a Java Spring-based microservice.

Advanced distributed training techniques, such as tensor train and tensor train with mixing, have been able. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by the limitations of implementing them in popular deep learning frameworks. Consequently, there is a lack of research exploring the potential of trainable commodity tensor structures in deep learning. This study delves into the capabilities of linear classifiers in space-form commodity tensors and establishes a fundamental principle that enables the extension of such classifiers to higher-order tensor structures. Furthermore, it presents a method for efficiently training linear classifiers within commodity tensor structures using random projections and explores their potential applications in distributed learning.

In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy, the density of stars is so great that gravity dominates their motion, resulting in an intricate orbital patterns. This area, known as the strong separation regime, is complex due to the stars' irregular shapes and varying motions, limiting analytical and numerical modeling attempts so far. Researchers obtained exact solutions for the stars' arrangements in this region by applying a novel Hamiltonian perturbation approach, taking into account the effects of a rotating galaxy. Their findings reveal how the stars' orbits are linked under these conditions, addressing a long-standing mystery in the field. By incorporating the stars' physical characteristics and the galaxy's structure, the model enables the calculation of the stars' orbital periods, distribution types, and the maximum number of stars in the surrounding area. Compared to previous studies using simplified models, the current model performs better in predicting the observed periodic variability in the peacock nebula and the ratio of the number of stars at certain distances from the black hole in the omnibus galaxy.

This paper introduces a method called RMPM, a variant of model predictive control, which uses random models derived from set-based models through parametric variations. By considering this approach, RMPM generates optimal strategies based on probabilistic predictions of future states and controls, thereby avoiding issues associated with non-convex optimization. A practical illustration of RMPM is provided in this study.

Independent component analysis is utilized in various real-world applications such as brain-computer interfaces and gene expression studies. The existing ICA research primarily focuses on the assumption that data is drawn from a fixed, known set of sources. In reality, source distributions often need to be learned from limited sample data, which can lead to inaccurate results. This research introduces a novel sparsity-promoting approach to ICA that does not rely on knowledge of the source distributions. The proposed method leverages the principles of compressed sensing and theoretical guarantees for successful signal recovery. Experimental outcomes further validate the efficacy of the approach.

To account for the disparities in species populations, we utilized a species-projective dynamics on the S^2 sphere, incorporating features of both the voter model and the neutral invasion biology. This approach allowed us to analyze a species competition model with a novel mechanism, namely a competition-colonization tradeoff, through which species thrive both in crowded environments (competition dominance) and isolated areas (colonization dominance). This species competition model was found to exhibit chaotic behavior, particularly in certain singular boundary equilibrium scenarios. We discovered that species coexistence is achievable through two primary methods: (i) a basic strategy involving the creation of diverse population distributions; (ii) a complex interaction dynamic, resulting in the emergence of an intricate, highly irregular species network. Notably, the species competition model's dynamics diverged from those of established voter model and neutral invasion biology responses.

We investigated the category of regional von Neumann algebras within the context of abelian quantum double models and found that it forms a monoidal category that is non-degenerate but lacks a unit object. Additionally, we determined that the category is equipped with a braiding system.

To enhance the magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in a cavity magnomechanics system, we introduce a concept called coherent feedback. By implementing a quantum circuit that reconnects the system in a non-trivial manner, we simulate its effects on the evolution of the cavity magnomechanics model. This circuit enhances the entanglement among the modes, surpassing the performance of the optimal local optimal classical feedback. Moreover, the increased entanglement results in enhanced advantages for applications such as phonon-number squeezing and photon-number correlations. This innovative coherent feedback technique has the potential to be applied to various controllable quantum systems.

We've developed a comprehensive compilation of single-particle collinear splitting operators at the one-loop level for QCD within a dimensional analysis framework. These operators are defined with respect to short-distance physics and are expressed in terms of logarithmic variables that appear in spinor configurations. The full set of operators includes those associated with quark and gluon particles, as well as a crucial top-quark sector, which we've added to the existing literature. The underlying calculation involves a double-bremsstrahlung process in scalar QED and we've adapted this to the case of massless fermions, as well as massive fermions with general ratios of internal to external momenta. The resulting splitting operators are presented in a universal form, applicable to a range of dimensional analysis schemes including $\beta$-functions, hard-collinear and soft functions, and we've verified our results against known data in various cases.

The Neron Desingularization (Neron + Desing) algorithm was first introduced by
Gabriel and Herrero as a vector space decomposition method. This was later
developed into a constructive procedure by Montel and later by Gabber and Ramero.
The positive General Neron Desingularization (pGND) algorithm is an extension of
the Neron Desingularization algorithm, applicable to one dimensional local rings.
The pGND algorithm demonstrates the existence of a sequence of finitely generated
free modules, analogous to the Neron Desingularization steps, in the context
of one dimensional local rings with specific module properties.

Ancient sundials held significant cultural importance in interpreting time across diverse civilizations. As the primary time-telling device before the widespread use of mechanical clocks, sundials also played a crucial role in Indonesian history, particularly during the classical age. As the sun's movement was observed and noted for religious and scientific purposes. This research aims to document and study Indonesian sundials, known as 'urat api,'in order to revive knowledge from various islands and establish a digital database to collect societal insights. The project also examines the potential applications of artificial intelligence in sundial documentation and heritage preservation.

This research introduces a novel integrated surface-based communication and brain-like information network, where D2D reflection surface communication is used by machines to reflect and enhance brain-like information exchange. A comprehensive model is developed to analyze the integrated system, which is based on a refined version of the Integrated Information theory in the context of neural networks. This expanded theory takes into account the effects of reflection surface paths and brain-like information network topology, as well as the varying brain area strengths. To quantify the integrated system's functionality, the theory defines a concept called Alpha-Integrated Information. We derive a systematic approach to optimize the parameters of the integrated system for maximum Alpha-Integrated Information, which is affixed to a reflective surface. Numerical results illustrate the feasibility of the proposed system and show that the optimized solution has fewer network data rate requirements compared to non-optimized cases. Furthermore, the theoretical and numerical findings demonstrate that the integrated system's Alpha-Integrated Information can be enhanced when all nodes on the reflection surface are actively engaged in communication.

The conventional use of LDV involves manually moving the probe in three-dimensional space to obtain two-dimensional velocity distributions. This approach relies on human operators taking individual decisions based on real-time data, which can lead to inconsistent results. This work explores the effectiveness of implementing LDV systems in complex flows, specifically focusing on the control of a single-point LDV system to obtain two-dimensional velocity distributions. To optimize the probe's position, we employed different decision-making strategies, including random, pre-programmed, and adaptive methods. The constant flow of particles was modeled using the Ingram-LDV model, which enabled us to develop an adaptive optimization algorithm based on the particle's expected lifetime. This adaptive algorithm resulted in a 30% reduction in positioning errors and allowed us to collect high-quality data in turbulent flows with low-to-medium Reynolds numbers with minimal positional variations. However, positional variations became more significant in high-Reynolds number flows, which indicates the need for further refinements to the algorithm.

The paper explores an alternative approach to classical first-order logic by incorporating relationships between models to alleviate the limitations of the Tarski Urquhart parameterization. This revised framework incorporates "dual relationships" between models to counteract model-theoretic shortcomings of the Tarski Urquhart parameterization. Consequences of this change include dual model completeness, complete indeterminacy, and the inclusion of the lattice of classical propositional formulas within the lattice of dual relationships.

The effectiveness of programmable phase discs in correcting various types of aberrations in transmission electron microscopy is being explored. We demonstrate that a phase disc can be designed to mitigate the effects of focus, astigmatism, and high-order spherical aberrations, including those of order 3000. Through simulation, we show that multiple phase discs can be utilized in series to eliminate all forms of underfocus, including phase contrast. This approach offers an alternative to existing solutions such as post-column aberration correction and lens design modification for aberration compensation.

In the context of assessment, calculators are indispensable tools, enabling
students to concentrate on computational challenges rather than struggling
with mechanical calculations that can hinder their understanding. As the
stakeholders in assessment, we need to decide whether specific calculators
are necessary or not, which involves evaluating their capabilities and how
they integrate with the content to be assessed. This study aims to provide
clarification on how to determine the required calculators for different
mathematics subjects at various levels of study.

The problem of counting walker positions during a d-dimensional random walk within a unit sphere in the L1-norm has been considered. We have derived expressions for calculating the number of walker positions in each dimension, which allow us to compute the total number of distinct positions in the d-dimensional space.

The total number of distinct positions in the d-dimensional space can be calculated by taking the product of the total number of distinct positions in each dimension, which are 3^d, 5^d, 7^d, 9^d, 11^d, 13^d. We have also provided a theoretical explanation for these results using modular arithmetic.

We have utilized the fact that in a d-dimensional random walk with a single step of size s, the possible positions can be represented as the sum of s times an integer vector with a specific number of non-negative components. Therefore, the number of positions depends on the number of such integer vectors with a specific non-negative component count.

We have derived expressions for the total number of positions in the d-dimensional space by calculating the total number of integer vectors with a specific non-negative component count, which can be either 1 or more. This calculation involves the use of a generating function that encodes the total number of positions in the d-dimensional space for each value of s.

By applying the GOP approach to spin foams, we've developed a new polymer black hole model with expanded geometry, which incorporates not only thermal radiation but also dynamic processes giving rise to real and complex quasinormal modes. Building on the ANTOP method, we've calculated the quasinormal spectrum of the $l=2$ fundamental EMICW mode, predicting a spectrum of $n_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu = -2dx^2 - 2\mu dh^2$ influences on the spectrum. The influence of quantum hair on the spectrum due to the nonvanishing quantum magnetically of the black hole appears to be minimal but may become more pronounced at higher orders.

We have developed a theoretical approach for studying the thermal responses of Dirac materials like graphene, gapped graphene, and carbon nanotubes through their specific heat capacities. By incorporating both electromagnetic and phononic interactions, we've devised a framework that allows for temperature-dependent gap creation and an analysis of how this affects the materials' thermal properties. In the case of graphene, we find that strong coupling with phonons eliminates the gap created by doping at high temperatures, leading to a characteristic energy scale related to the sound speed in the material. In carbon nanotubes with chiral properties, we observe the emergence of multiple gap states due to the spinning motion of electrons, which can be gapped by laser light. The specific heat capacity of carbon nanotubes exhibits a unique transition at low temperatures, diverging like the square root of temperature, and is amplified by the presence of electron spinning. Ultimately, we argue that our findings provide a universal explanation for the unique thermal responses of graphene, gapped graphene, and carbon nanotubes, grounded in the universal physics governing Dirac cones and sound waves in these materials.

The quality of automated phone calls can be enhanced by using speech synthesis, but it is challenging to accurately predict the context of the conversation to achieve the best results. A novel approach called MaskedDialogue uses a masking technique to mask portions of the previous conversation and obtain predictions based on the remaining context. This method is efficient as it only requires minor changes to the existing speech synthesis model and allows for direct training on conversational data. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that MaskedDialogue significantly improves speech naturalness and conversational coherence when compared to other top-performing speech synthesis systems.

A recent advancement in statistical modeling called projection predictive inference offers a versatile approach to machine learning problems. This method extends beyond traditional Bayesian methods to handle non-Gaussian models, however, the increased computational burden limits its practical application to problems with relatively few data points. A modified version of projection predictive inference, hidden space projection predictive inference, successfully tackles high-dimensional data issues by utilizing a low-dimensional latent space representation to achieve scalable computation. When compared to other subdimensional approaches, hidden space projection predictive inference demonstrates superior performance while providing more accurate results. A comprehensive evaluation of hidden space projection predictive inference is carried out on various data sets, showcasing its capabilities and efficiency.

Advances in machine learning have propelled it to become the cornerstone of internet security, with adaptive systems able to evolve in response to changing environments. However, machine learnings' reliance on data makes it vulnerable to attacks centered on manipulating training datasets. While attacks on machine learning systems are typically categorized as either targeted or untargeted, a new approach has emerged that combines these elements: it's possible to train a malicious model that can manipulate input data both to divert labels and to generally increase the output's predictive inaccuracy. Our study shows that this type of attack is viable across a wide range of models, datasets and scenarios. To counter this type of attack, a new adversarial testing framework has been developed that's capable of discovering malicious patterns within trained models.

Climate change denial has become a pressing issue in the digital landscape, with vast networks of misinformation spreading via social media. Through an examination of Twitter conversations, this research reveals the scope and character of climate change conspiracy theories, including their dissemination by automated accounts, and identifies the subjects of these conspiracy theories. Furthermore, the study compares the levels of engagement generated by mainstream and conspiracy theory-related content, and uncovers the practices of conspiracy theory promoters. The findings of this research will serve as a foundation for the development of effective strategies to counter climate change deniers on social media.

A comprehensive search is conducted to identify a novel matter form, referred to as "shadow matter," using data collected by the CMS experiment for 138 million proton-proton collisions, occurring at a 13 TeV energy level. Shadow matter is predicted to interact with ordinary matter only through elastic forces and is anticipated to manifest as a single top quark or a pair of top quarks following a different trajectory due to diverse interactions with "ordinary" matter and possible distinct decay modes. The "ordinary" matter interactions result in "ordinary" decay modes being suppressed, thereby increasing the likelihood of observing the suppressed decay modes. Two potential scenarios, corresponding to different "ordinary" matter interactions, are taken into consideration while conducting the search. In both scenarios, the "ordinary" matter interactions cause the suppressed decay modes to be higher for a single top quark than for a top quark pair. In both scenarios, the "ordinary" matter interactions cause the suppressed decay modes to be greater for a single top quark than for a top quark pair. In both scenarios, the predicted rates for detecting "shadow matter" are lower than the rates predicted by the CDF search. In both scenarios, the predicted rates for detecting "shadow matter" are lower than the observed collisions data. In both scenarios, the predicted upper limits on the cross-sectional rate for producing "shadow matter" in proton-proton collisions, occurring at a 13 TeV energy level, are lower than the predicted rates previously reported by the C

Given a category with n-exangulated triangles, represented by a linearly generated n-exangulated subcategory of a permutation abelian category with n-Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality, we demonstrate that the category itself possesses Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality. Conversely, under the scenario where a category with n-exangulated triangles includes Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality, we establish that its corresponding subcategory of linearly generated triangles exhibits n-Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality. Moreover, we show that, in cases of n=1 and n=2, this duality criterion can be restated using respective categories of n-permutation abelian subcategories of triangle subcategories. Additionally, we provide a number of detailed examples to illustrate our findings.

Building upon the influential paper by Imbens and Wooldridge, 2006, this research further develops the theoretical framework for a specific case of instrumental variables analysis. The paper demonstrates that under the assumption of a single individual choice, the expected outcome value from administering multiple treatments can be effectively made singular, thereby simplifying complex equations. Utilizing this theoretical framework, the paper reexamines the returns on investment in various college majors and finds strong positive outcomes associated with degrees in engineering, economics, and law, alongside negative outcomes associated with degrees in humanities and social sciences.

A recent study proposes establishing a research facility near a low-background site to create a high-accuracy antineutron and hyperon physics experiment. The concept involves creating a 50-megaelectronvolt beam of antiparticles using a high-accuracy antiproton beam from a future Circular Electron Positron Collider. The potential experiment could achieve groundbreaking precision in measuring the antineutron's mass, a crucial parameter for refining the nuclear and particle physics understanding of the universe. Furthermore, the experiment is expected to make significant contributions to understanding the properties of a positively charged particle called the delta isomer. The proposed experiment has immense potential to advance knowledge in various fields of physics including hadron physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology.

Theories surrounding the equal mass distribution in hierarchical triple systems remain unclear, particularly when considering systems that consist of a binary with a third body orbiting it. Our research provides additional insight into this phenomenon by exploring the impact of disk interactions between the binary and the third body. Our findings show that in tandem with the binary's orbital period, the binary's center of mass moves towards the third body due to gravitational interaction, resulting in a shift towards the equal mass distribution. A comparable process occurs when the binary's plane aligns with the third body's orbit, due to the binary's center of mass accelerating towards the point where it is farthest from the binary's plane. When considering systems where the binary's plane is perpendicular to the third body's orbit, a mass transfer between the binary components may also contribute to this equal distribution. A graphical tool that calculates the system's evolution over time in both scenarios is provided, including how it relates to the binary's orbital period and the binary's semimajor axis when considering a plane aligned with the third body's orbit.

This article examines flat cosmology models based on a lattice theory to describe the universe's theoretical framework. The article discusses the inherent characteristics of these models in the context of a de Sitter universe, proving that any lattice-based flat cosmology results in a de Sitter space. It also explores the likelihood of these models representing the universe's fundamental theory, addressing potential issues with time and UV divergences within the framework.

This study presents an innovative variational image modeling technique that integrates image segmentation and restoration methodologies. Our image model combines principles of Mumford-Shah, Plateau, and minimal partitioning theories to optimize divide-and-conquer strategies. By applying the nearest neighbor minimization method, we can break down complex optimization issues into more manageable local minization problems. Our approach is versatile and can be adapted to accommodate various cost functions, region merging, and splitting heuristic methods, thus enhancing its robustness and efficiency. Our scientific contributions lie in developing a powerful image modeling tool that facilitates the automatic construction of a discrete partition and its corresponding mapping, which is highly beneficial for a wide range of applications, including image information extraction, object counting, geographic information system integration, and image recognition.

Active supermassive black holes, which include massive quasars, may have a unique characteristic feature known as superradiance. This phenomenon, caused by the resonant interaction between a black hole's spinning accretion disk and waves, can lead to the rapid growth of a new, unstable mode consisting of waves and the black hole's spinning counterpart. As the spinning black hole undergoes superradiance, its spin may decrease, reversing the usual expectation that black holes lose spin in accretion scenarios. The rapid changes in black hole spin could potentially be detected in data collected by the Gaia spacecraft, which tracks the motions of billions of stars. Researchers have analyzed the distributions of black hole spin in two sets of simulated quasars and found that the distributions' mean spins change dramatically at a critical mass threshold of around 10^9 solar masses. Additionally, the possible existence of ultralight dark matter, which can also cause superradiance by accumulating near a black hole, has been considered. However, the simulations suggest that the resulting changes in black hole spin would be less pronounced than those seen in massive quasars. Consequently, the observed lack of highly spinning black holes among the simulated quasars suggests that superradiance related to accretion is a more significant factor than superradiance caused by ultralight dark matter until a more detailed theoretical understanding of dark matter is established.

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Brian simulator and seamlessly integrating with existing workflows. This emulator successfully emulated error-free neural network behavior on the Loihi processor, which was further validated by running a complex neural network prototype on it.

A solar noise storm is created by intense plasma phenomena on the Sun, typically situated in or near magnetic free spaces. Solar noise storms are notable for producing strong radio emission that can be observed at powers of tens to thousands of watts per square kilometer. The development and dynamics of these storms are closely tied to changes in their surrounding magnetic field structures. For a particular storm studied in this paper, researchers have discovered an unusual pattern in which the area of the storm and its radio emission power exhibit a distinct relationship during a small flare that occurs within it. Initially, the flare causes the area of the storm to decrease due to the concentration of plasma within smaller regions of the storm, only to then expand as hotter plasma moves in. Concurrently, the storm's radio emission power experiences a significant increase during this process. This discovery reveals new insights into how the magnetic field structures of these events evolve and provides further understanding of the complex processes involved in the dynamic behavior of these rare solar phenomena.

A discussion on the principles behind an innovative type of optical trap has been presented. This new design improves upon conventional optical traps by allowing for a planar configuration of the trap, thus enabling greater integration with other devices on a chip. As a result, we anticipate that this technology will contribute to the development of more sophisticated chip-based devices in the fields of magneto-optics, superconductivity, and quantum information processing.

The spherically symmetric interaction between a massive black hole and a vast, rotating, collisionless gas is investigated. This gas is initially confined to a finite, concentric sphere around the black hole. As it nears the event horizon, the gas undergoes a radial acceleration, losing both kinetic energy and angular momentum due to the black hole's gravitational influence. As the gas enters the transition region adjacent to the event horizon, its internal structure becomes increasingly ordered, largely retaining angular momentum. As a result, a significant portion of the gas's total angular momentum is captured by individual particles, eventually becoming bound to the black hole as tidal disruption fragments into multiple, tightly orbiting circles. A portion of the captured fragments displays measuring rotation patterns within days following the disruption, indicating that the particles have completed multiple orbits around the black hole. Estimates suggest that particles completing ten or more orbits around the black hole retain at least 90% of their initial angular momentum. This study indicates that during accretion, a significant portion of the captured material can take on various, short-to-medium period rotational characteristics, influencing the growth of a black hole through accretion while also producing distinctive observational features.

The rate at which a moving atom gives off electromagnetic radiation is examined,
with the atom positioned near the surface of a narrow mirror. When the atom
moves at a slow speed, the strength of the electric fields that interact with it
is minimal, but as its speed approaches a significant portion of the speed of light,
the strength of these fields significantly grows. Under these conditions, the atom's
movement causes an increase in the rate of electromagnetic radiation emitted.
Consequently, fast-moving atoms can emit more energy in the form of radiation
than stationary atoms, contrary to expectations. This phenomenon has implications
for our understanding of the relationships between speed, charge, and mass.

The massive young cluster Westerlund 2 (Wd2) in the cluster's central area has a distinct lack of red supergiant stars (RSGs), which is unusual given the cluster's age and location. This non-standard behavior could be attributed to several factors, including an outlier population of RSGs that reside outside the cluster core. Utilizing archival data from the VISTA Survey of the Southern Galaxy for the Mid-InfraRed (VVV), we were able to detect 14 RSG candidates positioned outside a 10 arcminute radius around Wd2. This number exceeds the cluster's core by 7, showcasing a significant dispersal of these stars outside the cluster's central area. By cross-referencing the VVV data with the Two-Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer's All-Sky Catalogue of targets for the Near-Infrared, we were able to verify the 14 RSG candidates and rule out any potential background contamination. This enhanced the cluster's core by 4 and cut down the population by nearly half. By analyzing these results in conjunction with the distribution of a red Asymptotic Giant Branch star in the area, we suspect the presence of a population of RSGs that reside outside the cluster's central area. This paper introduces an advanced deep learning approach designed to enhance the visual quality and readability of handwritten document images, especially when they're heavily damaged by noise, deterioration, and overlapping text. Unlike existing methods that focus solely on visual improvement, our network uses both a generative adversarial network to produce higher-quality images and a separate task to remove unnecessary text from scanned documents. By incorporating multiple outputs, our network can generate refined images that not only look better but also improve readability. We tested our approach with a large dataset of real-world documents and achieved remarkable results, with over 98% accuracy in removing unnecessary text and a 20% gain in readability on handwritten text recognition systems.

Indonesia's largest island, Java, has implemented an ID card extraction system utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology to facilitate processing and data sharing across government platforms. Building upon existing Java-based software, our enhancement involves fine-tuning OCR results with rule-based analysis to achieve better extraction results, especially for sections facing difficulties with OCR. Our improved Indonesian ID card extractor has demonstrated superior outcomes, not only outperforming its predecessor but also achieving high accuracy rates for all card details, even when presented with imperfect scans. Furthermore, our open-source code on GitHub now offers the complete source documentation for easy reference.

In vehicular communications, the IEEE 802.11p standard plays a crucial role in system performance, yet it suffers from significant channel estimation errors due to its shortcomings. To overcome this problem, a Temporal Smoothing LSTM-based Channel Estimation (TSLCE) method is presented, employing a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for 802.11p channel estimation. The proposed TSLCE method first leverages temporal smoothing technology to transform raw channel impulse response into a stable form, then utilizes an LSTM network to perform channel estimation. Performance evaluations demonstrate that the TSLCE method achieves improved root mean square error reductions of approximately 90% and enhances channel estimation accuracy by about 25%. Furthermore, the TSLCE method showcases enhanced vehicular communication capabilities in terms of accurate channel-based channel equalization, precise bit detection, and reliable data discarding.

Ancient astronomers left behind a legacy of magnificent drawings depicting planetary systems, matches of the heavens, and the cosmos, which have survived to this day. These colorful artifacts, however, have typically been restored for museum purposes, thereby losing their original historical value. To rectify this, we introduce an innovative approach that uses Generative Adversarial Networks to colorize and enhance historical astronomical images while maintaining their original features. To the best of our knowledge, this method marks the first attempt to apply this technique to restoring ancient astronomical drawings. By testing it on the famous Harlow Shapley Atlas and the Tycho Prairie-Yale Reflected-light Survey, we demonstrate its effectiveness and the precision gained in image restoration. The code supporting this research has been made publicly accessible at its GitHub address.

The successful application of neural networks in real-world scenarios heavily relies on their ability to accurately solve complex problems, whether it be classification or a non-linear regression task. Typically, neural networks achieve optimal results through a combination of iterative weight adjustments and non-linear activation functions. Inspired by the Universal Approximation Theorem, this proof of concept aims to demonstrate that a simple neural network with a limited number of layers can solve intricate functional problems without relying on gradient-based optimization methods. By utilizing only input-output data, the weights within each layer are calculated directly, eliminating the need for iterative processes and pseudo-inverses, which could lead to numerical instability issues. Our results show that this structure has the ability to accurately replicate complex functions despite the presence of noise in the training data. Additionally, our approach is characterized by its computational efficiency for large and complex datasets.

This transfer report outlines the accomplishments of the ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCC) from 2021 to 2022. The committee's structure, purpose, and methodology are described in detail. ECRCC successfully carried out various tasks, including organizing young researcher-focused workshops, creating resource lists, and developing policy papers. The committee also played a key role in developing multiple ECFA reports and provided feedback to late-career researchers through mentorship training. To address the concerns of early career researchers, particularly regarding publication and career challenges, the committee initiated an email discussion thread and gathered input from the community. The committee expressed its concerns regarding these issues in an open letter to ECFA.

Recent breakthroughs in nanotechnology have brought forth dual metastructures with concurrent left- and right-handed properties, which have been shown to affect both optical and radio waves in the same way. Research in the optical realm has been hindered by the absorption of metastructures themselves, limiting practical applications. This study proposes a method to control line waves using dual metastructures without using antibodies, utilizing a small gap between parallel plates instead to achieve stronger interactions and higher optical field enhancements. By designing this gap as a resonant cavity, it's possible to achieve further amplification of line waves at specific frequencies. Computer simulations demonstrate that by adjusting line wave phase and amplifying optical signals, dual metastructures can be used to control line waves effectively, opening up new possibilities in the optical domain.

Human-robot cooperative autonomy is gaining momentum, driven by techniques like learning, specifically multi-agent learning. This approach leads to more accurate and efficient learning outcomes. The primary obstacle to implementing multi-agent learning is the substantial computational resources required. As a result, only a few private institutions can engage in such research, limiting its scope and restricting the exchange of knowledge. To overcome these challenges, a cognitive framework is needed that can leverage distributed computing capabilities, enable scalable and versatile multi-agent learning tasks, and facilitate the collaboration of AI researchers. This paper introduces such a framework, allowing for the preparation of learning tasks through dialogue-based inputs and the execution of training processes on cloud-infrastructure or edge devices with local resource allocation. The benefits of this framework include increased computational power, more variable and adaptable learning tasks, and enhanced collaboration among researchers. The multi-agent learning approach can now be applied to complex tasks, even on devices previously incompatible with such projects, like popular robotics platforms. The implementation details and performance of this framework are demonstrated with a fully functional integration of a local human-robot cooperative multi-agent learning task on Ubuntu Linux operating system and Microsoft Azure cloud-infrastructure.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the average absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.

The quality of a Knowledge Graph (KG) is significantly influenced by the accuracy of its links, which can be enhanced through link prediction. This research investigates how link prediction can support relation extraction, a crucial task in NLP that identifies relevant relationships between entities in a text to generate KG edges. We analyzed three link prediction methods and discovered that leveraging their predictions could increase the precision and recall of relation extraction models by up to 6.25% and 5.75%, respectively. To achieve better results, we developed a dual-learning approach combining existing KG information with annotations from relevant datasets. Furthermore, we found that integrating link prediction into KG embedding models via knowledge awareness yields superior outcomes.

The persistence of quarkonium in a high-temperature and dynamic environment is of great importance. In this study, we have calculated the melting temperature of quarkonium states in a hot and anisotropic QCD environment for various values of momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential. Using an energy distribution function based on quasi-particle Debye mass, we have obtained binding energies of quarkonium states in both longitudinal and transverse directions. These calculations follow the experimental observations of the finite spatial momentum on the quarkonium states in the same context. The findings are compared with the previous studies in the same context but without momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential. The influence of momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential on the binding energy and the stability of quarkonium states is also discussed.

Our study focused on the internal magnetic fields and arrangements for the chains in Tb3RuO7. We used neutron-diffraction experiments to determine the internal magnetic fields and arrangements for the chains in Tb3RuO7. We found that the internal magnetic fields vary evenly between 3.9 and 5.2 Tesla and exhibit no correlation with the L-values of the chains' magnetic arrangements. The latter showed antiferromagnetic patterns with 90-degree angles for chains 1 and 2, but an irregular arrangement for chain 0. It displayed magnetic bonds with lengths of 3.9 Angstroms in the ab-plane and exhibited no magnetic ordering itself, but influenced the surrounding chains had exhibited magnetic ordering. Our data reveal that the irregular arrangements of the chains' magnetic bonds are attributed to the irregular internal magnetic fields. We analyzed the effects of the internal magnetic fields on the arrangements and found that our results are in agreement with our theoretical calculations.

Machine learning models can learn representative features within their internal layers, but these are often non-interpretable. We present a novel method that enables machine learning models to develop interpretable representations within their internal layers. Our approach Modulated Recurrent Activation learns local functions within select layers by exploring relationships between input features and output values. By employing a guided learning technique, we converge towards the desired representations while incidentally learning the relevant input features. These new representations significantly improve the models' predictive capabilities and facilitate generalizable, interpretable features that can be applied across diverse datasets.

Using causal inference techniques, we develop a novel method to tackle covariate-shift problems in supervised learning by leveraging information from both causal "what-if?" and causal "what-caused-it?" dimensions. This novel approach fuses predictive modeling with information-theoretic arguments to derive a learnable bound on prediction uncertainty. As a result, we propose the Semi-Generative Epistemic Uncertainty Model (SGEUM), a versatile tool that can be trained end-to-end using existing optimizers to tackle covariate-shift problems in both classification and regression tasks. Our experimental evaluation compares SGEUM to established methods and reveals significant enhancements in robustness against covariate shift, particularly in regression tasks. Furthermore, we provide additional experimental scrutiny to demonstrate that our method effectively incorporates both causal dimensions in its training and utilizes the entropic structure of its epistemic uncertainty to make more informed predictions.

In the realm of deep learning, encompassing neural networks and statistical learning, we are witnessing unprecedented breakthroughs. However, the fundamental geometric structures underlying these breakthroughs remain obscure, even as experts acknowledge their importance. This research seeks to illuminate the geometric frameworks at the heart of deep learning innovations. By combining elements from quantum information theory, operator theory, and nonlinear algebra, we reveal the connections linking geometric structures to the efficacy of deep learning models. Along the way, we introduce novel mathematical concepts, such as noninear modes, which encompass divisors on a projective variety, and "Hankel nonstandard modes," enabling the generalization of standard modes. The mathematical frameworks developed here find applications in studying the spectral properties of graphs, such as those arising from random matrix theories or the graphs representing datasets. By exploring the local Fourier transform, we gain insight into the spatial arrangements and patterns within datasets. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between certain geometric structures and the principles of linear system resolution and information retrieval. By delving into the geometry of specific neural networks, such as the ResNet, we gain a deeper understanding of the relationships between geometric structure, computational complexity, and model efficacy. Ultimately, we offer a unified theoretical framework, known as Geometric Deep Learning, encompassing the various geometric structures presented here, as well as the relationships between them.

Identifying the ground-state distribution is a challenging aspect in Quantum Many-Body Physics, especially in high-dimensional systems where computational methods struggle to converge. We employ the principles of Variational Inference to develop a theoretical framework evaluating the variability of iQSD and iQFT variational states, thereby providing an indicator to pinpoint the ground-state region in the parameter space. This concept is exemplified through its application to the 1D transverse field Ising model and the 2D Jaffe-Grassberger model.

A key challenge in interpreting machine learning models lies in understanding their decision-making processes, especially in complex high-dimensional environments. Although variable importance methods have been effective in highlighting individual factors influencing model choices, they fall short in providing a comprehensive understanding of the model's decision-making process, particularly in advanced models. To bridge this gap, we have developed a novel LRP-based method that effectively decomposes the jet classification decisions made by multilepton, boosted decision tree decision trees, and residual neural network models. By doing so, we gained valuable insights into which input variables the models use to make accurate classifications, ultimately leading to refined selections in the multilepton model and new observations about the CNN layers' preferences for color, position, and intensity of the input particles.

For every positive r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into subsets containing at most r consecutive elements. Numbers in this series have recently been studied in relation to a mathematical formula that describes the growth of a plant's fructification pattern. To further generalize this concept, we're introducing new parameters called degenerate r-linked Stirling numbers of the second kind. These parameters represent the number of ways a set can be divided into distinct, non-empty subsets, where each subset has at most r consecutive elements. We've developed closed-form expressions for these new parameters using a combinatorial method that incorporates the concept of lattice paths. Additionally, we've established a recursive relationship for these parameters by applying a common technique in enumerative combinatorics. We're also providing alternative representations of the parameters by refining the concept of degenerate k-Stirling numbers. To establish this relationship, we've developed closed-form expressions for these new parameters by applying the concept of lattice paths in a different manner.

In a recent study, a category of layer symmetry groups was discovered, which consists of double-gray layers and their associated monoids. This research paper delves into the subjects of irreducible representations, location symmetry groups, and various layer organizations within a two-dimensional torus. Specifically, we explore the irreducible modules of the latter group and establish a full classification of location symmetry induced representations of four distinct types of layer symmetry groups. Additionally, we present relevant examples and suggest potential future areas of investigation.

For a Killing vector field with a closed, timelike curve trajectory on a Ricci flow solution, we demonstrate that its associated impulse operator still has a geometric interpretation in terms of the Ricci flow solution's metric. This is because the operator can be expressed as the sum of two vectors derived from Killing vector fields with non-closed, timelike curve trajectories. This implies that these vectors maintain their connection to the Ricci flow solution's metric as well. This finding generalizes a previous observation made for stationary black holes.

Developing an accurate machine learning model for a highly complex system like the Hubbard model has been a significant challenge, as the model's signs on wavefunction components create numerous local minima, making optimization difficult. Researchers have employed complex-valued neural networks as a potential solution to this problem. By training such a model with an extremely large dataset obtained through Monte Carlo simulations, scientists have successfully constructed a wavefunction consisting of two sign-free components, achieving results comparable to best available bounds for small systems. These findings suggest that complex-valued neural networks can potentially resolve the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo methods, enabling the accurate computation of wavefunctions for systems with numerous interacting electrons.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the flavor symmetry is identified as an $U(1)$ subgroup of $Sp(6)$. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken, leading to nonzero masses for the standard model fermions. A mechanism proposed here allows for a significant mass difference between two pseudoscalar NG bosons to arise, even with $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry, which proves beneficial in avoiding large flavor-violating decay modes for the pseudoscalar. Furthermore, a flavon-controlled mass generation mechanism for the right-handed top and the topological Chern-Simons interaction is introduced. A flavon-based model for the hierarchy of Yukawa couplings in the third family is proposed, which incorporates a $U(1)'$ gauge boson and includes the first principle analysis for the stability of the the vacua.

The concept of virtual reality's shadow aspect refers to the unobtrusive ways its influence is perceived. As VR becomes increasingly integrated into various fields including science, education, and industry, research has uncovered several subtle psychological effects that can clarify and expand its definition. We have identified two primary types of these subtle effects - influence and substitution. Influence refers to situations where VR's impact is recognized, whereas substitution occurs when VR poses as a solution despite actually being the root cause of a problem. Notably, the boundary between these two categories is often difficult to determine, as seen in the common case of eye strain in VR, which goes unacknowledged though clearly present. Another example is the satisfaction felt when engaging in VR, which can both be and not be a shadow aspect. Furthermore, we drew parallels between the shadow aspect of VR and Candor Keck's 'penumbra and umbra' model for understanding surprises, which helped us systematize various subtle effects of VR's influence. By classifying these effects into influence, substitution, and pseudo-shadows - a new category that includes deceiving indications of VR's true influence, we have created a comprehensive list of all identified subtle effects.

We examine how the choice of model and adaptation method impacts the performance of low-resource language models when adapted for use in previously unseen languages.
