In a new study, we identify a key relationship between the quantities of energy admitted and absorbed in a randomly scattering system. By combining this discovery with existing knowledge of linear subspaces, we develop a comprehensive theory for tracking energy transmission and storage within complex systems. Furthermore, our research confirms that a selected pathway for energy transfer exists and can be pinpointed in any scattering system, giving rise to theoretically optimal designs for energy harvesting.

Researchers have identified a previously unrecognized spiral feature in the outer region of the Milky Way galaxy. The newly detected 3-kpc arm, which exists at a specific velocity of about -100 km/s, is situated between two existing spiral arms, known as the 4-kpc arm and the Carina Arm. These three features form a clear pattern in the galaxy's velocity map provided by the HI4PI map. The estimated age of the 3-kpc arm is relatively young, approximately 13.4 million years. It's believed to be oriented nearly perpendicular to its current position due to warping, and its presence contributes to the overall exponential shape of the galaxy's disk. The feature can be seen at a specific longitude in the HI4PI map, which corresponds to a position where the galaxy's disk appears pinched. This observation suggests that the 3-kpc arm has contributed to this characteristic. The feature can also be seen at a specific longitude in the CO map from the Green Bank Telescope. The observed material from the 3-kpc arm exhibits relatively high temperatures, which could be due in part to the galactic bar. The estimated mass of gas in the 3-kpc arm is about 2.7 x 10^5 solar masses. The galactic spiral structure is discussed in the light of the new discovery.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover diverse solutions. In this study, we evaluate whether multi-solution optimization is more effective than single-optimization by analyzing variety in simulated annealing and genetic algorithm's performance. Our results show that while multi-optimization may be preferred due to a higher likelihood of overall model accuracy and more versatile applications, single-optimization offers a higher solution quality and greater variety in its optimal solutions. Additionally, our results indicate that the benefit of multi-optimization is most apparent in scenarios with non-uniform fitness functions.

We investigate the 3D Roommates problem where individuals have preferences that can be broken down into cumulative and evenly increasing components. These preferences are admissible due to their nature, ensuring that any corresponding 3D housing arrangement would be collectively rational and satisfy the condition of positive sum satisfaction. To address this challenge, we develop two polynomial-time algorithms: one can create a fair and rational allocation using random assignments of rooms, incorporating factors such as room sizes and individuals' cumulative preferences. Another algorithm takes as input a pair consisting of an additive and a discrete preference profile over a set of agents and their corresponding room capacities, and produces a corresponding assignment that satisfies all three conditions - to be fair (i.e., maximal), rational and satisfying sums positively.

A new study is conducted to examine the impact of distinct electron-phonon interaction mechanisms on valley physics in two-dimensional materials. The analysis focuses on a single band with symmetry-allowed electron-phonon interaction, involving either diagonal or off-diagonal mechanisms. The research shows that when the phonon frequency is much higher than the electron's kinetic energy, the latter's transverse motion is minimally affected. Conversely, when the phonon frequency is on the same order as the electron's kinetic energy, the latter's transverse motion is noticeably damped. The findings indicate that the influence of electron-phonon interaction on valley physics largely depends on the relative magnitude of these two quantities.

The Gromov-Hausdorff distance brings geometrically related metric spaces closer together. We've discovered that the set of all such spaces, paired with real numbers, forms a complete metric space. Additionally, our research finds that certain categories of metric spaces are comparable to each other in terms of the GH distance, and are thus equivalent to the category of complete and uniformly convex metric spaces. We've also found that certain metric spaces have the property that their scales do not decrease when embedded in the GH-balls of other spaces, and that the diameters of their images in the GH-bounds of other spaces are bounded.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with wide bandwidth and a large spatial coverage is presented. The antenna's specified parameters include a 3-dB bandwidth of 11% and a broad spatial coverage of 3-dimensional (3D) |S11|-10 dB, spanning from -90 to 60 degrees in phi and -30 to 130 degrees in theta. To achieve its operational specifications, the antenna's microstrip feed was calibrated to operate at 28.25 GHz, which is the center frequency of its 3-db bandwidth. The calibrated antenna achieved an average broad spatial coverage of 4 sigma squared, equivalent to a large spatial coverage of approximately 60 x 60 inches (152 x 152 cm), which far exceeds conventional antennas' operational ranges. A detailed analysis based on calculated 2D and 3D |E|^2 distributions, along with the calculated beamwidth and broad spatial range, confirms the designed antenna's wide bandwidth and large spatial coverage operational capabilities.

The integration of reinforcement learning coders with fault-tolerant quantum computing allows us to combine the advantages of both approaches in developing reliable quantum systems. Traditional fault-tolerant coding methods are excessively resource-intensive due to their need to verify and retransmit faulty data. Employing reinforcement learning coders, which efficiently encode information by leveraging the current state of the system, can significantly reduce this burden. We're examining variants of these coders, including an optimization method that optimizes performance based on the likelihood of data corruption. This optimization leads to a performance equilibrium where the coder's error rate matches the existing noise level, ultimately resulting in negligible performance loss. We've successfully applied this coding approach to the compilation of quantum algorithms for preventing quantum information leakage in superconducting quantum processors. The findings show that this coding technique leads to considerable cost savings in qubit resources for a specific quantum algorithm, indicating its potential to automatically adapt and enhance the fault tolerance of quantum algorithms for various applications.

Quantum-enhanced metrology has consistently shown its capacity to exceed classical limits, however the advantages are typically tied to specific experimental configurations. This research investigates the capabilities and limitations of dual-cavity quantum metrology setups, including systems with and without automatic stabilization through laser feedback. For both scenarios, we derive optimal bounds for the phase sensitivity for both coherent and entangled initial states. This study reveals that entangled initial states can achieve optimal sensitivity only if the cavity coupling is much stronger than any decoherence effect affecting the system. Furthermore, we show that phase sensitivity can be significantly improved with the assistance of quantum feedback, a result which holds true for both coherent and entangled initial states. Lastly, we compare our findings to the capabilities of advanced phase-sensing tools and show that quantum-enhanced methods can outperform them when implemented in a dual-cavity setup.

Research has examined photon-hadron correlations in Au+Au and d+Au collisions at a 200 GeV energy level. In Au+Au collisions, direct photons are dominant at high $p_{\rm T}$ values above 6.5$-$8.0 GeV/c. The photon-hadron correlations in d+Au collisions resemble those from peripheral Au+Au collisions, indicating that cold nuclear matter effects are primary in peripheral Au+Au events. Calculated photon-hadron correlations were also compared to data from the most central Au+Au collisions, revealing discrepancies between measurements and simulations. The results suggest that the collective behavior cannot be solely accounted for by initial energy release or other jet-interaction phenomena.

The emulation of quantum many-body systems on near-term quantum devices is essential to bridge the gap between current technology and fully-fledged quantum computers. However, the diverse types of quantum systems make it challenging to pick the most suitable platform for simulation. In this study, we explore a hybrid approach that leverages both digital and analog quantum computing to tackle complex fermionic systems. By combining the fermionic matrix product state method with the bulk fermionic code, we demonstrate the ability to handle extensive fermionic systems despite limited qubit resources. We illustrate the efficacy of this hybrid approach by successfully simulating the Heisenberg ferromagnet's spin collapse and the Lieb-Lininger model's one-dimensional antiferromagnetic coupling on a 26-qubit analog quantum processor enhanced with 12 classical degrees of freedom.

A long-standing issue in machine learning has been to achieve good performance in both optimal solution quality and generalization abilities. Numerous studies have made efforts to resolve this dual goal, though it's challenging to make general claims due to the diverse approaches. In this paper, we propose a new method for creating extensive feature sets that enable improved large-scale optimization outcomes and generalization performance. Our method incorporates three key components: 1) generating abundant features, 2) identifying essential features, and 3) enhancing feature resilience. By producing an abundance of features, we can find the most crucial ones at the feature level, and leverage these features for robust model training. Notably, our approach features feature selection as a primary component to demonstrate optimization-generalization performance enhancements. Through thorough experimentation on quadratic optimization problems, we've found that our proposed method produces an abundance of features resulting in superior generalization capabilities and better solution quality compared to the current benchmark methods.

A versatile framework utilizing a fuzzy logic control (FLC) framework on a single-layer modeline (SLM) has been developed for generating three-dimensional tissue patterns with multiple complex structures. The proposed multi-structure model, which incorporates a novel FLC-SLM design, achieves concurrent shaping of multiple structures within a single volume. The algorithm's iterative process allows for simultaneous adjustment of light patterns to create and maintain multiple structures. The proposed framework's performance is demonstrated using various examples of 3D tissue patterns with multiple structures such as helices, layers, and intersecting spheres, with an added benefit of maintaining an optimal light power level under real-world conditions. The proposed framework's capabilities are then demonstrated in real-time experiments using 405nm UV light on 1% and 2% agarose gels. The results showcase its ability to create an interwoven pattern of red and green helices, with an excellent agreement between simulated and actual light patterns. The study provides a reliable method for generating and organizing multiple structures in real-world tissue patterns under real-world conditions.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency using existing data. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we demonstrate that our DRGE estimator has asymptotic consistency under weaker assumptions, supported by a novel proof. Additionally, the support restriction of DRGE can be relaxed to include unbounded policies, improving its efficiency compared to CGE under this relaxation. Finally, we explore the future potential of combining DRGE and CGE in a Bayesian context.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth of a CLICTD monolithic small collection-electrode technology demonstrator using the INKA test stand at DESY, and compare it to thick sensors on fully functional CCSDA+ devices and high-thickness CCSDRC devices. Results show that the active sensor depth of the CLICTD technology demonstrator is approximately 30, in good agreement with the 30 epitaxial layer. Moreover, the team discovered that the charge collection efficiency decreased by around 50% due to the reduced sensor thickness. Nonetheless, the study suggests that the lower power consumption of the CLICTD technology could offset the decreased charge collection capability. Additionally, the study evaluates the performance of CLICTD monolithic planar hearing-aid device, which features a hearing-aid compatible design with large collection electrodes. Although the charge collection capability is limited by the thin sensor, the results demonstrate promising features, including high spatial resolution, selectivity, and quiet-time rates. Finally, the team explored the charge collection capabilities of CLICTD monolithic small-pin technology, which is designed for space applications and characterized by narrow, rectangular pins. Although the charge collection capability is limited by the thin sensor, the results showcase excellent one-dimensional resolution, quiet-time rates

A new development in high-resolution imaging technology is the rapid atmospheric self-coherent camera (RASCAM) technique which builds upon the principle of speckle imaging. By coherently detecting the residual speckles in an adaptive optics system's beam, RASCAM delivers sharp images of the target, even in the presence of speckles that have been partially controlled by adaptive optics. This process eliminates the need for an additional laser and moves towards a data-driven, in-situ approach to achieving higher resolution. We report the first laboratory demonstration of RASCAM's capabilities, using the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Testbed (SCEAOT) and an industrial-grade camera, to showcase its effectiveness in maintaining a high level of image sharpness even when facing increased atmospheric turbulence. Furthermore, RASCAM successfully maintained its image quality at a level comparable to speckle-free conditions, despite the introduction of more intense atmospheric speckles.

This study presents a novel exogenous kernel for the CIR model to accurately simulate negative interest rates in a realistic, easy-to-understand framework. Unlike previous kernels based on Cox et al.'s (1985) work, our approach avoids the reliance on artificial measures such as square root of absolute covariance processes. Our method integrates the advantages of the Euler discretization scheme and a pre-conditioning technique developed in Lord et al. (2017). The solution allows for high precision solutions with a time step much larger than the Courant number. Our kernel maintains the square root of absolute covariance process's non-negative value, ensuring the model's applicability to extreme scenarios with minimal impact on the underlying stochastic process. Practice-oriented numerical examples are provided in the appendices.

Long-established theories requiring sterile neutrinos include the Ba-Bar anomaly and matters associated with non-zero billiard table dimensions. Large-scale experiments such as DUNE are potential game-changers in enhancing our understanding of neutrino oscillations. This research investigates DUNE's capacity to detect long-range neutral-current interactions that signal the existence of sub-eV sterile neutrinos. By leveraging DUNE's extensive perspective and the LHC's comprehensive coverage, we are able to comprehensively map potential sterile neutrino parameter spaces. Our analysis demonstrates that DUNE can effectively explore vast areas of sterile neutrino opportunity, particularly in vast regions of long-range neutral-current parameter space. Furthermore, we find that DUNE and LHC joined forces can extensively cover sterile neutrino parameter spaces even in the presence of existing KATRIN constraints.

Meta-analysts conducting mixed-effect research aim to integrate disparate findings to draw more comprehensive conclusions. The current methods employed in mixed-effect analyses often overlook random subject-level errors, oversimplify other variables, or limit the number of available studies. To address these shortcomings, we have developed a new estimation method called the sturdy cluster estimator. This method enhances traditional pool-to-pool meta-analysis by accounting for both treatment and subject-level variability across studies. The sturdy cluster estimator's reliability has been confirmed through theoretical assessments and real-world applications involving a bivariate meta-analysis. When applied to a dataset of 16 studies focusing on the relationship between the HDL and LDL levels in response to conjugating esterification with lipoprotein particles, the sturdy cluster estimator revealed a 0 and 0.98 percentage increase in the estimated correlation coefficient and a 0.23 units increase in the estimated slope, respectively, when compared to a conventional estimation method. Furthermore, we have established that our estimators display robustness in the face of biased sampling and rarefied data.

A novel numerical approach is introduced for simulating complex single-phase flows where small particles interact with a dominant fluid. The method utilizes a Lagrangian framework with particles whose trajectories are calculated over extended periods. When particles collide with each other or the surrounding fluid, their movements are paused and resolved using a revised solver that accounts for the specific physics at play. Post-collision, their paths are re-evaluated. We compared this approach to the conventional Lagranian method that uses time-steps and found that it permits larger time-steps for particle collisions without losing accuracy, thus improving computational efficiency. Additionally, we observed that both methods can accurately model particle movements during non-collision scenarios. We conducted a series of tests validating the new approach, including collisions between particles and the surrounding fluid, multiple particle collisions, deformed particles and moving boundaries. The results from these experiments match the findings from the established Lagrangian method. Furthermore, the new approach performed better than the traditional time-steps method in scenarios such as the collision of two particles and the shaping of a particle by the impact of a moving droplet.

Unruh's observation that accelerated particles can't be in a global superposition of momentum states has been supported by multiple analyses. However, this observation can't be confirmed empirically due to the lack of detectable radiation. A new interpretation of Unruh's observation provides insight into its underlying meaning. This interpretation indicates that Hawking radiation is an illusion born from the interplay of measurement-induced wave function collapse and the infinite number of degrees of freedom in vacuum states. Consequently, the notion of radiation emerging from black holes through Hawking process loses coherence, revealing a more complex reality where vacuum states possess a rich structure far exceeding human perception capabilities.

We examine the transverse momentum imbalance created by nucleons in the direction perpendicular to the collision plane using the color dipole description. By combining this with calculations of momentum distributions of nucleons and final-state interactions, we develop a theoretical framework to investigate how momentum imbalances of individual nucleons contribute to the overall transverse momentum of the final state and learn about its dependence on the momentum transfer via $Q^2$. Our results indicate that the longitudinal momentum of the final state is primarily determined by the sum of individual nucleons' momentum imbalances, although the transverse momentum is largely generated through final-state interactions. By focusing on the impact of a single nucleon's momentum imbalance, we find that the contribution from the struck parton itself dominates before being surpassed by contributions from the other nucleons at higher values of $Q^2$. Furthermore, we find that the transverse momentum acquired by the other nucleons increases with $Q^2$ and is proportional to the square of the momentum transfer in a logarithmic function of $Q^2$. Using quantitative estimates based on small-x calculations, we find that the average transverse momentum acquired by the other two nucleons is approximately 150 MeV at $x_{\rm Bip}\sim 0.3$ and increases to 200 MeV at $x_{\rm Bip}\sim 0.9$. This study presents whole number solutions for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ under the condition that $a\neq 0$. It has been demonstrated that there are two cases which can provide whole number solutions: the first case yields an infinite number of valid solutions when $n$ is even, whereas the second case yields a single solution when $n$ is odd. Notably, all whole number solutions obtained from these cases can be expressed as a product of two matrices.

When a liquid flows through a channel with varying cross-sections, it exhibits
destabilizing behavior, resulting in the formation of droplets at locations where
the channel narrows. This study focuses on a specific scenario where a liquid stream
enters a channel and analyzes the conditions that lead to droplet fragmentation.
We've developed a theoretical model based on the Lagrange-Euler map and an
energy-based approach to determine the threshold for droplet fragmentation.
Consequently, we've derived an asymptotic expression that depends on the fluid
dynamics and geometry of the channel, which aligns with our previous theoretical
findings for a particular geometric case. Moreover, we've established that the
droplet fragmentation process can create smaller droplets and even individual ions
depending on the initial liquid droplet size and channel geometry. Finally, we've
related our theoretical model to recent experiments and discussed the practical
implications of this work.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on non-volatile storage for critical data protection. Crash consistency in non-volatile storage has made significant progress but remains unsolved for complex workloads, particularly those involving algorithms with covert dependencies. These hidden interdependencies can lead to data corruption and render the crash recovery process unreliable. The vulnerability of algorithms to data corruption at crash time not only affects the data integrity but also requires the development of more intricate recovery algorithms, increasing complexity and requirements. Our solution introduces an algorithm-guided crash reliability framework, allowing users to specify potential data corruption and customize recovery probability, thereby simplifying the development of reliable algorithms and enabling us to explore new possibilities for designing such algorithms.

The issue of mapping structures in information networks is a fundamental challenge, with significant implications for applications such as discovering patterns in consumers' buying habits or analyzing genetic relationships. However, the large scale of modern information networks presents a major obstacle, making it essential to employ efficient algorithms that can take advantage of available resources, such as parallel processing capabilities, to achieve optimal performance. This paper introduces DistMC, a versatile system designed for mapping structures in large information networks across various domains, by leveraging the power of inference engines and parallel processing frameworks, such as Hadoop and GPU clusters. To illustrate its capabilities, DistMC is applied to the analysis of a massive social network with over 600 million users and an evolving network tracking the spread of scientific papers across more than 15 million nodes.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the performance of various regression models and a novel statistical theory, called Flux, for predicting the unstable binary asteroid (153211) 2006 SY67's orbital evolution. To enhance precision, we refined the Flux model's initial forecasting parameters using 20,000 binary trial systems instead of just 50. Despite these optimizations, the Flux model still struggled to accurately forecast the primary population's 1σ and 2σ errors for the w-plane coordinates, with mean absolute errors of 0.161 and 0.231, respectively. In contrast, a straightforward multivariate linear regression achieved better results, with mean absolute errors of 0.045 and 0.063, respectively. Furthermore, the improved Flux model performed best among statistical models, but still underperformed the regression model. Based on our findings, we believe the enhanced Flux model is a promising approach, but it requires further improvement to overcome the limitations of statistical forecasting.

Data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC for PbPb collisions in 2015 were used to evaluate the production rates of J/$\psi$ and $\chi_{c}$ in lead-lead collisions. The measurements for PbPb events were compared with those for p-p collisions, resulting in a 5.02 TeV lead-lead collision dataset that included over 7 million events. The study accounted for variations in photon momentum and hadron production rates. The effectiveness of the bottom-quark recombination process in reducing the yields of prompt charmonium was assessed, and the phenomenon was found to dominate suppression effects below 2 $R_{AA}$ units. Furthermore, the investigation revealed that recombination contributes to the suppression of a portion of the light charmonium (primarily feed-down from heavier states such as $\chi_{b}$), which is referred to as prompt charmonium loss. To distinguish between prompt and nonprompt contributions to suppression, the authors applied an analysis that compared $p_T$ distributions of $\mu^{+}\mu^-$ and $D^0\mu^-$ pairs. The outcome indicated that the majority of the suppression at 2-5 GeV/$c$ and high $p_T$ is attributed to nonprompt mesons.

We propose a formal framework for continuous models by leveraging the principles of category theory. This involves defining a category whose objects represent models and arrows represent embeddings. Building on the existing framework of Ben-Yehuda et al., we develop a theoretical structure that incorporates class formation systems, establishes a suitable equivalence relation, and defines essential morphism properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the category over which we establish a database theory is equivalent to a subcategory of a specific category of ordered structures.

The velocity of project development in the modern era is directly tied to how test cases are prioritized, particularly when it comes to identifying cases that cover new functionality and address issues reported by users. This paper demonstrates a parallelized implementation of a valuation-based selection algorithm for test cases, leveraging the speed of CPU processing via hyper-threading. By breaking down test case attributes into distinct value groups, the algorithm distributes similar tasks to different threads, effectively minimizing the time spent on each sub-task and thereby achieving a linear time complexity for large datasets. This pioneering approach effectively accelerates test case selection, enhancing the overall efficiency of the framework's development process.

A new form of deep neural network is proposed, which can process data in the form of sequences and multiple sources, enabling the learning of complex and representative patterns. This is achieved through the design of a Deep Sequential Network with Multiple Inputs (DSN-MI), comprised of multiple parallel parallel temporal memory cells that receive data from various sources. By utilizing the multiple inputs to each cell and its past performances, the network can uncover hidden patterns across different data streams. This is demonstrated through applications such as the detection of suicidal thoughts in patients based on electronic health records, emergency calls, and social media posts. Experimental results reveal that the proposed solution surpasses existing alternatives in predicting suicidal risk.

Our research reports a definitive outcome from the Chandra and XMM-Newton space telescopes' joint observation of Cassiopeia A, along with the results from the Chandra/XMM-Newton/IXPE joint-toothless observation of this supernova remnant. Our study focused on the very energetic rays emitted by the remnant's core, which is the leftover of the massive star that exploded. Specifically, we recorded the polarization of X-ray light emitted at 3-6 keV within a tiny 2" radius area centered on the remnant's core. Our sensitive measurement indicates a significant polarization of $6.1\pm0.9$% at 95% certainty, which supports the theory that the major explosion force responsible for the core's ejection came from the rapid spinning of the core's material. Additionally, our results from IXPE, XMM-Newton, and Chandra at 5-6 keV show a notably lower polarization of $0.7\pm1.1$%. Our findings support the concept of two types of energy release occurring at the core of supernovae, namely the rapid spinning of the core (resulting in the highly polarized rays) and the interaction of the core with nearby gas (resulting in the loosely polarized rays).

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ where all elements are distinct and positive. We're looking at the minimum requirement for $n$ such that it's possible to select $a_i$ values whose sum equals any given integer from 1 to $a_1 + \ldots + a_n$. Erdos originally inquired about finding the lowest possible $n$ for the scenario where all possible sums are unique, which led Motzkin to introduce additional constraints to explore non-integer element sets, which have since been further modified by several mathematicians. This paper presents yet another advancement in this line of inquiry.

Measurements of the sound speed in dense stellar matter have revealed details about the equation of state in compact star interiors. Research on the sound speed and its relationship with density and pressure as well as energy density has been conducted, followed by an assessment of the sound speed's causal and adiabatic properties. Furthermore, equations of state that include the presence of dense matter with strangeness as well as baryon number density are examined, with consideration given to three distinct forms of dense matter strangeness: bag-like, H-disk, and quark matter. Our analysis indicates that the sound speed's behavior largely depends on the mass of the compact star and its generated pressure, and shows that the causality constraint has a more significant impact on the causal equation of state at lower densities, while the adiabatic constraint has a greater impact at higher densities. Additionally, our findings suggest that quark matter equations of state result in the smallest sound speeds and causality violations at lowest densities.

We investigate the impact of discrete squeezing transformations on the optical field, specifically how it affects the field's quantum fluctuations in the Fock basis. The application of a nonlinear squeezing transform results in a non-uniform distribution of field energy across the Fock basis, leading to variations in fluctuations depending on the basis number. Furthermore, we find that nonlinear squeezing can either reduce or increase the field's anti-correlation properties relative to a vacuum state, contingent on the Fock basis number. Additionally, we demonstrate that combining squeezing and displacement has a cumulative effect on the field's quantum fluctuations.

The interfaces between gas and liquid phases in two-phase systems serve as hyper surfaces, which require in-depth characterization to extract relevant information for various applications. This paper introduces a technique for generating skeletons from interface data, which provides a simplified representation of hyper surface structures, ultimately leading to more efficient and adaptable solutions. The proposed skeletonization method is adaptable to different interface representations and allows for the detection of features without the need for prior knowledge. Furthermore, the technique can be combined with techniques for extracting closed structures, which will be discussed in a companion paper.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit motor activity by rolling across the cellular surface via symmetrical membrane remodeling processes. This behavior facilitates virus propulsion through mucus and enhances infection efficiency by enabling the virus to travel along cellular protrusions. A recently developed model for viral motor function in C-respved viruses is being adapted to include the role of capsid elasticity. This revised model predicts that increased capsid rigidity actually enhances viral motor speed, contrary to expectations. However, higher levels of viral elasticity may lead to abnormal viral shapes and impaired motor function. Furthermore, introducing fluctuations in viral size could potentially cause malfunctioning viral motors to recover by increasing their operational speed. Although the proposed model focuses on C-respved viruses, its underlying mechanics are likely applicable to a broader range of enveloped viruses.

Galactic warping provides essential insight into the interactions and dynamics of galaxies that reside in groups and clusters. High-resolution optical studies reveal two primary types of warpages: M and U shapes. The deformed disk galaxy project utilizes a large dataset of M U-shaped galaxies drawn from the SDSS, consisting of 844 galaxies in total. By combining optical data with multiple fiber information from the SDSS, we calculate the mass distribution of galactic halos and investigate their relationship with galactic properties. Our initial findings indicate that galaxies exhibiting U-shaped warpages have larger galactic masses compared to those with M-shaped warpages. Furthermore, we observed a U-shaped galaxy's orientation in the galactic plane correlates positively with the galactic disk's minor axis, implying that U-shaped galaxies tilt equally in all directions. To explain the unique behavior of U-shaped galaxies, we propose a theory stating that U-shaped galaxies are star-forming galaxies that lose their balance due to the interaction with the galactic disk. The distinction in galactic orientation, coupled with the variation in galactic masses, suggests that galactic warping is influenced by a diverse range of mechanisms, including galactic friction, the attraction of galactic halos, and tidal forces.

This paper proves that on a complete non-compact n-dimensional manifold, if the Ricci diminutors increase the scalar curvature and a given function meets specific criteria, then the scalar curvature remains constant. Consequently, we have derived a new proof of the Liouville Theorem for complete gradient shrinking Ricci solitons with constant scalar curvature and demonstrated that this result implies an extension of the original Liouville Theorem for complete gradient shrinking Ricci solitons presented in Nguyen and Zhang's work.

A comprehensive structure and phonon properties investigation has been carried out on the cubic compounds $ABi_{2}$ with $A=$ K, Rb, and Cs via abnormal Raman scattering measurements and ab-initio calculations. The latter revealed that the substances crystallize in a specific type of $Cmcm$ structure. This finding, however, contradicts earlier X-ray data which indicated that the compounds adopt a tetragonal structure. A thorough investigation of the structural properties revealed that the underlying cause of this discrepancy is the interference of chiral modes in the Raman spectra, resulting in the hidden degeneracy of the optical phonons. Two Raman peaks in the frequency range of 50-100 $cm^{-1}$ can be attributed to an accidental degeneracy resulting from the combination of phonon branches in the finite cluster. This phenomenon persists in the calculated and experimental results, allowing the effects of chiral modes to be determined. Meanwhile, the optical phonons exhibit a significant anisotropy in response due to the influence of the $A$ cation. Ultimately, the chiral mode in the cubic structure has been identified and its manifestation in the phonon anisotropy has been demonstrated.

We introduce a nonadiabatic version of Born effective surface and volume capacities in metals, particularly relevant to the transport of uncorrelated or short-ranged electrons. By combining nonradiative and radiative contributions, our approach provides a unified understanding of the Drude weight in terms of volume, surface, and interfacial capabilities. Focusing on nonradiative processes, our model demonstrates that the Drude weight is proportional to the volume capacity plus twice the surface capacity, with the surface term reflecting interfacial electron reflectivity. For three-dimensional metals with clean surfaces, the surface capacity dominates, offering insight into the inverse problem of optimal surface states for absorbing light. Moreover, our theory generalizes Born effective surface capacity to capture the contribution of multiple band states.

Following the model of d'Obrenovic, Bocabi and Breugem, it is argued that the the nature of turbulent flows can be understood by considering both the thermal disturbance and the behavior of the thermal spectrum. It is proposed that the thermal spectrum can be broken down into three distinct ranges characterized by different types of turbulence: a smooth and uniform area far from the source, a middle region affected by thermal disturbance, and a highly turbulent and disordered space close to the source. By analyzing these ranges, it is possible to gain a deeper understanding of the dynamics of turbulent flows, particularly the behavior of waves at the interface of the middle and disordered regions where the turbulence assumes a glass-like structure.

Three-dimensional topological insulators with time-reversal symmetry exhibit unique properties that originate from their geometric structure. When subjected to a magnetic field, these insulators display magnetoelectric effects, characterized by sensitive responses to the magnetic flux. We investigate the geometric magnetoelectric effect in a model of a three-dimensional topological insulator with a physical gap, showing that it exhibits nonlinear properties. By introducing magnetic monopole charges and applying an electric charge to the system, we demonstrate the occurrence of the Witten effect, where the magnetic monopole receives an electric charge proportional to the square of the magnetic charge. Furthermore, our findings for the geometric magnetoelectric effect agree with those of recent theories, and we also observe that our results conform to the requirements of the Chern number in the quantum anomalous Hall effect.

In delayed feedback systems, a small variation in the feedback path can drastically alter the system's dynamics, leading to enormous growth of initial disturbances. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in systems with periodic basic behavior, where short-lived and extremely large fluctuations occur, ultimately resulting in the system's instability. For the first time, we present a general approach to identifying and maximizing these massive amplifications. Our method is demonstrated using a mathematical model of a delayed laser system, which shows how tuning the system's parameters can greatly increase the effectiveness of feedback, often to the point of amplifying small disturbances by a trillion-fold. This discovery opens up new opportunities for delaying the onset of instability in sensitive systems and potentially exploiting these massive fluctuations for innovative applications.

We extend the random lambda calculus to incorporate explicit substitutions, 
then develop a global semantics for this modified calculus by drawing on ideas 
from ordered sets and lattices, similar to the study by Bonsangue and Brodsky. 
Unlike previous models, our global semantics naturally includes infinite trees, 
enabling us to construct a successful model for the multiplicative linear logic 
without the $\bot$-elimination rule.

According to current AI interpretations, robustness in artificial intelligence refers to the ability of models to produce the same output given varying input changes. In this research, we redefine this concept by examining if design dialogues can conclude successfully despite the designer introducing new information that does not affect the final outcome. The conclusions are that even seemingly robust designs are not robust to changes in user specifications and that the robustness of artificial intelligence, as currently understood, is not a reliable indicator of the robustness of design conclusions.

A possible explanation for the universe's initial conditions emerges from combining a quantum measurement of a holographic field immediately following inflation. The measurement causes a sudden and permanent distortion in the field's wave function, giving rise to the Higgs-Goldstone field that underlies both particle masses and the vacuum's non-zero energy density. The initial fluctuations giving rise to particle masses occur at energies linked to the inverse distance between the detector and the boundary, while lower energy fluctuations giving rise to the Goldstone field persist to the present and are responsible for the universe's non-zero energy density. Notably, these initial conditions arise from a quantum measurement, characterized by a non-zero probability of over-shooting the equilibrium value, thereby avoiding an infinitesimal amplitude that would not give rise to gravity. The model accurately predicts the relative magnitudes of the Higgs and Goldstone fields. The model is also capable of explaining the origin of dark energy. Additionally, the holographic boundary distance can be interpreted as the age of the universe since the end of inflation. Lastly, the model predicts that gravity should weaken at extremely short and extremely long distances from the source.

Proximal methods in optimization have uncovered new perspectives in analyzing the behavior of trajectories along the sublevel sets of nonsmooth functions. Specifically, we investigate how these methods can be utilized to identify the sublevel sets of functions in an intrinsic manner on general manifold geometries. By leveraging the properties of proximal-stationary points, we define a broad class of sets associated with each function sublevel. Our key finding establishes that these set associations possess a significant characteristic - they are inherently manifold-dimensions - regardless of the functions they represent. Moreover, we present concrete examples illustrating that this characteristic is irreplaceable. Building upon this framework, we develop a comprehensive theorem describing the manifold structure of the sublevel sets themselves. Notably, this theorem achieves a comprehensive description when the functions in question possess specific properties of controllability and strong-convexity. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a fresh perspective on intrinsic sublevel-set structures, accompanied by a novel perspective on the behavior of trajectories along these sets, thereby bridging the gap between proximal optimization theory and classical nonlinear dynamics theories.

We are introducing a new concept of feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within the context of associative rings. A prime ideal in an associative ring is considered feebly $1$-absorbing if any three non-zero ring elements whose product is from the ideal's multiplication, also have their sum equal to $1$. The properties and characteristics of these ideals have been investigated and it has been established that feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals exhibit all the characteristics of universally $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Moreover, a feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a commutative ring is identical to a prime ideal that is also feebly $1$-absorbing.

We investigated branching fractions and form factor parameters for specific $B$ meson decays that occur at the $q^2$ peak of the $\rho$ meson. Our analysis relied on $B^0$ decay data from Belle II, with the recoil $B^-$ particle having one of three possible modes of decay: $\eta\pi^-$, $\omega\pi^-$, or $\pi^+\pi^-$. Following the application of signal and background reductions, our results for the relevant parameters were determined through a maximum likelihood fit. Our final estimate for the $B^0 \to \rho^+ \ell^+ \ell^-$ branching fraction is $4.2 \pm 1.1 \pm 0.7 \times 10^{-4}$. The form factor $f_+(q^2)$ was then compared to various theoretical predictions, showing increasing discrepancies between the data and predictions as $q^2$ decreases. Additionally, our analysis provided an estimate of the lepton flavor universality ratio, which is $R_{D/\tau} = 0.147 \pm 0.034 \pm 0.010$.

Our work addresses the challenge of identifying spectral objects, a crucial step
in survey follow-up activities. We develop an efficient and user-friendly software
for object identification, which can handle large datasets conducted in collaboration
between human observers. The code employs a versatile interpolation method to match
observed spectra with known templates, ultimately resulting in more accurate and
reliable associations between objects and spectral templates. To enhance accuracy,
the code utilizes a data-driven approach to adjust spectral templates and reduce noise
in large astronomical datasets. Furthermore, the code enables users to utilize a variety
of algorithms to cross-correlate spectra and assess the likelihood of object identifications,
as well as provide an estimate of the identification quality. We illustrate the code's capabilities
by demonstrating its application to spectral data from the TON 90 Telescopium nova.

In the pharmaceutical industry, numerous medications are interdependent, forming networks based on their complementary uses and opposing effects. Current approaches in machine learning focus on modeling individual drugs separately, disregarding the dependencies among them. Conversely, network perspectives consider the relationships between drugs, but are limited in applying this structure to learning from data. Our proposed method, CDS-NET, aims to score medication pairs by incorporating both the chemical structure and relational characteristics of drugs, facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of drug interactions. Leveraging the principles of chemistry and immunology, our approach can be interpreted as modeling the immunological response to drug molecules. By optimizing pair scores, we can select medication combinations with enhanced clinical outcomes, effectively refining prescription policies to boost patient health. Experimental results on an open-source clinical dataset demonstrate the superiority of our method in predicting effective medication pairs, outperforming baseline models that rely on individual drug features or graph-based representations.

The development of autonomous vehicles is advancing rapidly, with countries like China, the US, and Japan pushing the technology forward. This research focuses on enhancing the detection of road damage in vehicles from these three countries to improve overall performance. To achieve this, we applied a two-stage transfer learning approach, initially training a model on a large dataset and then refining it with limited high-quality images. The efficiency of this method was initially tested on single-image datasets and then on video data. The results show significant improvements in accuracy for all three countries.

Imitation learning has gained significant attention due to its potential to replace traditional, costly methods of training policies. However, the effectiveness of imitation learning relies heavily on the availability of high-quality demonstrations, which can be difficult to obtain, especially in complex tasks. This paper introduces new approaches to address these challenges by leveraging existing expert behavior within the same task, as well as from distinct tasks. For same-task learning, we develop an efficient method to extract maximum value from limited expert demonstrations when the state-space is large. This method integrates the distribution of past states and actions from the expert into the imitation learning process. For cross-task learning, we propose leveraging the underlying structure of actions to transfer expertise across different tasks. This proposal relies on the identification of sub-spaces of actions, where existing demonstrations can be imitated effectively, and then utilizes these sub-spaces across multiple tasks to generate new demonstrations. This work presents empirical evidence of successful imitation from a diverse set of benchmark tasks.

Intensified magnetic forces may have a significant impact on the formation of the very first stars. This effect could be particularly evident around a protostar born from the collapse of a massive molecular cloud, where the magnetic field's intensity causes the angular momentum of surrounding gas to subside, enabling the protostar to grow more efficiently. A study has examined how such a intense magnetic field affects the formation of solid particles within this system, suggesting that it results in fewer and larger dust particles forming more quickly. As a result, the dust particles cannot prevent or slow down the protostar's growth; in fact, the protostar develops significantly faster. The increased efficiency of accretion leads to a Population III star forming nearly 100 times more massive than our sun in just under 12,000 years, a significantly shorter time frame than estimated previously. The intensified magnetic field also has the effect of slowing down disk rotation speed near the protostar, effectively preventing the disk from fragmenting into multiple stars. The researchers conclude that such a magnetic field has a significant impact on Population III star formation, potentially rendering theories of the resulting stars' formation and properties obsolete.

In data mining, association rule analysis is often applied to extract meaningful insights from retail sales data. The core concepts of this analysis - association rules and confidence - were initially defined by Agrawal et al. and Mitchell, but it was later revealed that their definitions were flawed. The fault was eventually rectified by Klis, but the improved standard resulted in coexisting multiple methods for generating association rules. The simplest way to fix the issue would be to select the smallest possible bases for association rules, but there is also a more comprehensive approach proposed by Mitchell. The relationships between the different methods were explored through the lens of repetition and new frameworks were introduced to simplify the comparison. The association rule analysis was linked to concept lattices by Klis, but the connection was not yet complete. The completion of this connection was the key challenge addressed in this research paper.

Following the passage of Proposition 63 in California, convicted offenders were mandated to undergo mental health treatment as a condition of their parole. This study utilized a quasi-experimental approach to evaluate the effect of this treatment on mental well-being by comparing two groups: those required to undergo treatment and a control group of unconvicted individuals. The study found that requiring convicted offenders to receive treatment led to significant improvements in mental well-being as evidenced by lower levels of depression and anxiety, though the benefits were confined to those who initially adhered to their treatment plans. Crucially, improvements in mental well-being were linked to reduced recidivism rates, with those who received treatment exhibiting lower rates of parole violations. Notably, we found that the positive effects of treatment varied based on the type of crime committed, with benefits being most evident among offenders who had been convicted of nonviolent crimes. Ultimately, our findings suggest that imposing mental health treatment as a condition of parole can have lasting benefits for both the offender and society, though variations in treatment effectiveness based on the nature of the crime committed were also observed.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine their relationships with zeta functions, and investigate other key properties.

Radio maps are increasingly being used for applications such as wireless network planning, device location tracking, and surveillance. While existing methods create radio maps from ground-level surveys, they fail to account for changing wireless communication environments, such as construction sites or areas with high environmental signal loss. To address this limitation, we propose using autonomous drones to dynamically update radio maps in response to shifting environments. By equipping drones with wireless transmitters and receivers, we can simultaneously explore areas and collect channel sounder data, enabling the creation of accurate spatial channel maps. To leverage this information, we develop a spatial mapping algorithm based on k-means clustering, which effectively constructs radio maps and tracks changes in the environment. Experimental results using simulated data show a 30% improvement in clustering efficiency, along with valuable insights into radio map assessment.

This research presents an innovative approach to identifying anomalies in timeseries data through the analysis of their temporal properties. Anomaly detection methods currently available are often reliant on spatial features extracted from data. In contrast, this proposal utilizes the Temporal Gauge Probability Model, based on a Hidden Markov Model, to identify unusual patterns in dataset subsets. By generating a probability distribution for temporal transitions, the model effectively distinguishes between genuine and artificial data, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting anomalies. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates adaptability to various data types, as illustrated through applications to solar wind and traffic patterns.

This investigation into multimodal authentication centers on integrating audio, visual, and thermal cues collected from a single, accessible sensor – the smartphone or laptop's camera and microphone combination – gathering data through a simple, easy-to-use app. To boost the security of various systems requiring individual authentication, we thoroughly examined and combined the intrinsic values of these three modalities. Our findings highlight the advantages of incorporating thermal and audio features into standard visual authentication methods. A systematic evaluation involving 60 participants demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed authentication framework, yielding a remarkable 99.5% success rate. Our study's novel contribution lies in exploring combined audio-visual-thermal authentication, thereby filling a gap in existing literature, and meticulously calculating the optimal cost associated with this method.

Current state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition and translation systems are nearly equal in performance when tested on English data, but this results in subpar outcomes when applied to other languages. To boost the efficiency and effectiveness of these systems for languages with limited resources, we propose a simple data augmentation method that leverages existing labels from companion tasks. By making existing information more usable, this approach minimizes additional processing requirements. Our experiments demonstrate that this data enhancement strategy achieves notable performance improvements for speech recognition and translation, with only a small increase in computational cost. Furthermore, we found that applying this enhancement to adjacent frames has a positive impact on output quality.

This paper addresses the issue of estimating a population parameter in a mixed population, where we know the proportions of different components but not the individual values. It proposes a method for combining estimates from independent samples of mixed populations, where the proportions may vary. This approach is based on the principle of generalized maximum likelihood and involves calculating weights for each sample proportionality parameter to merge the results. The paper demonstrates that this method yields an unbiased estimator of the combined parameter and proves it achieves the maximum precision possible in this scenario. The method is illustrated using real-world data on the area of particles and the distribution of counts in microbial experiments.

Achieving privacy in big data has become a significant concern. Current differential privacy standards ensure that an attacker cannot determine if a particular data record has been included in a dataset, but this approach only protects record-level privacy. When attributes within records are dependent, standard differential privacy may be insufficient. For instance, releasing a count of students by age and degree status may reveal the degree status of individual schools. To address this issue, a new framework called one-sided differential privacy is introduced. One-sided differential privacy enhances the standard differential privacy but does not further protect record-level privacy. By incorporating a new distance metric dependent on characteristics, the one-sided differential privacy framework demonstrates that releasing degree achievement counts alongside age can maintain the confidentiality of individual schools. To accomplish this, the framework uses a sequence of released data and a leaking probability threshold. When the difference in sensitive attributes exceeds a certain value, the release of new information significantly surpasses the leaking probability, thus indicating a confidentiality breach. To calculate this leaking probability, the framework relies on the calculation of the probability distribution of counts in smooth differential releases. Through experiments in synthetic data, the framework determines the optimal releasing probability for minimum expected utility when the difference in sensitive attributes is small, as well as the feasibility of evaluating expected leaking probabilities within the one-sided differential privacy framework.

We investigated the organic molecules in the AS 209 gas disk using data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, which we obtained under the Molecules with ALMA at Planet Creating Scales (MAPS) project. Although we detected various molecules across the disk, we noticed a distinct decrease in carbon monoxide levels within the inner 30 AU, especially at 10-20 AU, which corresponds to the location of the protoplanet candidate massing about 10 times the mass of Jupiter. CO's decrease is significant, as it suggests this molecule has been removed or destroyed in some way. A few theories attempt to explain this phenomenon, including one that postulates the molecule has been processed into more complex organic compounds by the planet's radiation, while another suggests it has been consumed by the growing planet itself. However, if we consider only the total gas mass we see that neither of these scenarios can fully account for CO's decline. A closer look at CO's distribution shows it has decreased more than any other detected gas except for certain organic compounds. Yet, in terms of mass, these organic compounds do not make up the entire gas disk as often thought. A breakdown of CO based on temperature and velocity also shows it has fewer warm and fast-moving gas parts than other detected molecules in the inner disk. These findings call for a new understanding of the role organic molecules play in the coexistence of planets and their surroundings.

We prove the existence of a mild solution to a specific mean field game control problem in a Euclidean space with state constraints. To achieve this, we introduce a degenerate parabolic equation formed through the Fokker-Planck equation and a Hamilton-Jacobi-Viscoci equation, both subject to boundary conditions derived from the state constraints. Ultimately, we establish the existence of a limit trajectory for the associated ordinary differential equation as the time step tends to zero.

Studying certain types of stellar structures has led to a recent surge in research, particularly in the observation of stellar threads in the Milky Way. This surge is likely fueled by the discovery of the cosmic thread phenomenon via gaia data, characterized by densely packed, elongated regions of stars linked to the Milky Way's structure. However, the true nature of these stellar threads remains unclear. Through thorough analysis using the gaia data set, we re-examined the existing definition of cosmic threads and their association with the galaxy's center, identifying numerous regions of elongated star concentrations throughout the sky. Notably, these structures exhibit no distinct variation in distribution relative to the galaxy's center. Consequently, we conclude that cosmic threads are simply densely packed regions of stars, which may serve as useful indicators of the galaxy's structure, but not unique markers of the center or exotic celestial entities.

The visual discrepancy typically refers to an item's incorrect category due to confusing similarities across classes, such as a shirt categorized as a dress. Existing solutions for visual discrepancy have proven ineffective for fashion industry applications. To address this, we have developed Visual InspectOR (VICTOR), a novel model that leverages the power of attention to detect visual discrepancies. VICTOR was trained in a contrastive manner on a vast fashion dataset and further refined through self-supervised learning using data augmentation to effectively capture the complexities of fashion datasets. By incorporating multiple heads in its multi-head attention structure, VICTOR is capable of balancing visual features and semantic classifications, thus enabling it to effectively detect visual discrepancies while maintaining classifiability. Through comprehensive experiments on the widely-used Causal Learning dataset and an in-house dataset created from online fashion item descriptions, we demonstrated VICTOR's superior performance in predicting visual discrepancies and comparable or improved results for semantic classifications.

In recent years, research has expanded beyond traditional classical information theory, exploring theories of quantum information. This has led to significant advancements in the field. This paper reviews the current state of research in the theories of quantum information based on non-classical light. These theories have seen substantial advancements with various applications including fundamental quantum studies and practical use in experimental physics. The potential for ground-breaking breakthroughs continues to drive research in this area.

As the complexity of FL models grows, the communication phase can become the bottleneck due to inefficiencies in gradient sharing. This issue is highlighted by the current synchronous gradient averaging method, which necessitates a full gradient exchange and can result in significant delays. The introduction of a federated tensor board for FL models enables a more efficient communication protocol. By allowing clients to gradients accumulate asynchronously and transmit unconstrained gradients, a optimized communication protocol is achieved. This optimization is further enhanced by a novel batch size selection algorithm, which determines the ideal batch size based on the client's local data availability. The proposed framework is then evaluated under various distributed data scenarios, with experiments demonstrating significant reductions in communication rounds and phases compared to the conventional FL method.

This research expands the operational calculus of distributions, applying it to polynomial tempered distributions with hyperingular singularities. It achieves this by establishing a Banach *-algebra structure for this class of distributions and then developing a differential operator mapping. Furthermore, it specifies the inverse mapping for a broad class of differential operators within this context, ultimately leading to formulas for scaled and shifted operators.

We suggest a method to calculate the shadow dimension of compactified extra dimensions from the cross-sectional area observed in shadow maps. This concept applies to scenarios with stationary sources such as black holes. The notion is illustrated using a scenario with a four-dimensional observer viewing a two-dimensional extra space separated from their main dimension. The dimensionality of extra spaces beyond the shadow radius cannot be inferred; however, lower bounds on extra dimensions can be determined by combining the shadow dimension with the Primordial Black Holes solution to the Swampland problem. Furthermore, we propose a new explanation for the galactic rotation curves' slope change, attributing it to a change in the extra-dimensional topology or the material composition of the galaxy's dark matter. This consists of an extensive network of microscopic black holes.

A static liquid raft is comprised of a thin layer of fluid whose surface is trapped between two rigid plates, separated by a distance that is much smaller than the characteristic length of the films bridging the gaps between floating objects. When this gap distance is smaller than the persistence length of the films, which is a measure of elastic energy over length, the raft undergoes a fracture-like transition as the gap size approaches a critical value known as the 'fracture point.' At this critical point, the ratio of mechanical energy to the energy of cross-linking between films reaches a critical value of approximately four, marking the onset of a fractal pattern consisting of highly stretched films bridging isolated clusters of objects. Our findings apply equally to static and dynamic situations, with dynamic stability dependent on the balance between external forces and the elastic energy of cross-linked films.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of advanced GaN technology lies in reducing the hole mobility in p-type GaN. This problem can be tackled by modifying the strain within the material, which in turn affects the lattice parameters and electron density in the material. However, achieving just the right amount of strain can be a difficult and imprecise process. This research proposes an innovative approach to increase the hole mobility in GaN by aligning the material's lattice parameters to optimize performance. The proposed technique involves aligning the lattice parameters of the semiconductor material by introducing specific elements to fine-tune the strain and electron density within the material. For exemplary purposes, this research used ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ to demonstrate the potential for improved hole mobility by optimizing the material's lattice parameters and reducing activation energy requirements. The results showed that introducing these elements reduced the activation energy of GaN by 58% and increased the hole mobility by 200%, surpassing the current state-of-the-art mobility performance.

Marine robots face significant challenges in navigating through complex and dynamic environments, such as strong currents and thermal gradients that affect their buoyancy. Historically, Gaussian Processes (GPs) have effectively modelled these phenomena by considering spatial correlations, while other factors have often been disregarded. Nevertheless, GP regression suffers from a time or index shift issue, interpreting parameter values as relative rather than absolute quantities. Furthermore, GP regression models often result in smooth distributions that may not accurately represent the actual state space due to over-smoothing. To address these limitations, we introduce the Sparsified Gaussian Process Regressions (SGPR) approach, using multiple sources of information to determine the optimal correlation length scales through robust negative log likelihood optimization, thereby addressing the GP covariance matrix singularity and resulting in sparse posterior distributions that provide a more detailed understanding of the state space. By applying SGPR to low-frequency changes in sea temperature variations, we successfully conducted a sea temperature-based navigation trial, demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

This paper builds upon the findings of an earlier study (starting from page 385) to derive formulas for the Darboux and Calapso transformations of isothermal surfaces when expressed in linear potential form. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that a specific class of isothermal surfaces can be mapped to a particular subset of hyperbolic surfaces consisting of certain types of holomorphically stressed membranes.

We examine three distinct cases of nonparametric estimation for a single regression function and discuss how local averaging methods can influence its estimation. By conditioning on an optimal number of covariates and allowing the remaining variables to be used in the estimation, we can obtain consistent estimates of the regression function. Specifically, under certain conditions, these estimators demonstrate rate of convergence comparable to that of independent data estimation. Furthermore, our research explores the effects of dependent data on nonparametric estimation and extends the scope of applications for this method to include conditions beyond those initially identified in the literature. By doing so, we are able to provide more precise error estimates for our estimators. The specific results presented in this study pertain to conditionally linear regression models and smooth conditional variation scalar functions, which are estimated using kernel methods.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on modified $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We explore the $\lambda$-versions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and derive associated identities. Our work extends the initial research by Kim-Kim and we identify a distinct pattern within the derived identities. We also discuss the limit as $\lambda$ approaches $1$. Our findings are comparable to the results obtained by Kim-Kim for $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also provide a distinct pattern within the derived identities. We also discuss the limit as $\lambda$ approaches $1$. Our findings are comparable to the results obtained by Kim-Kim for $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

Static knowledge graph frameworks are frequently used to link unconnected entities but have not been widely applied to the task of predicting relationships between entities that do not currently appear together in a knowledge graph. Our research explored the feasibility of using these frameworks to address the challenge of link forecasting. We discovered that models traditionally used for link prediction in knowledge graphs can be adapted to this new task and developed an approach that utilizes static knowledge graph frameworks to forecast links between high-degree entities in a knowledge graph. Our experiments demonstrated that the combinations of adapted link forecasting models and static knowledge graph frameworks were capable of accurately forecasting links that were absent from a knowledge graph. Our proposed method specifically showed a 25.2% higher Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) than traditional link forecasting models on the Semanticscope knowledge graph. Our analysis further revealed that static knowledge graph frameworks are particularly effective when used to forecast links between two entities that have high degrees of connectivity.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs exhibiting infinite path connectivity, any equivalent C*-algebras derived from them undergo robust shift equivalence. This finding can also be restated as robust shift equivalence of C*-algebras corresponds to isotopy of corresponding graph invariants. Moreover, the article specificates conditions under which unifrom convergence of equivalent invariants implies robust shift equivalence of the associated C*-algebras. It further presents an example illustrating non-convergence of such invariants on graphs containing infinitely many infinite paths and shows that the current methods employed in inductive analysis yield exponential time complexity. Lastly, the article asks whether robust shift equivalence of C*-algebras implies shift equivalence of graphs, asking for a characterization of such equivalence.

Using the Markov chain Monte Carlo method within the general propagator framework, we investigate the distribution of heavy quark as a function of momentum and transverse mass at finite magnetic fields. We demonstrate how the non-zero magnetic field affects the fragmentation pattern of heavy quark by changing its distribution shape from isotropic to anisotropic, depending on the direction of the magnetic field relative to the quark's momentum. When the magnetic field is in the same direction as the quark's momentum, the distribution of heavy quark is found to be Gaussian in transverse mass, whereas anisotropic Gaussian or Gaia-like distributions are observed when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the quark's momentum. We further analyze the radii of the anisotropic Gaussian distributions in both in-plane and out-of-plane directions and find them to be decreasing functions of the magnetic field strength. Besides, the ratio of the in-plane radius to the out-of-plane radius of the Gaussian distribution is observed to be sensitive to the magnetic field, potentially serving as a key indicator of the existence of a heavy quark in high-energy collisions under extreme conditions.

To address the issue of language models struggling with question answering in cases where answers aren't included in the provided text, we suggest integrating knowledge graphs into the modeling process. By doing so, we train the model to infer missing information and make necessary connections, even in the absence of explicit text references. Empirical evaluation on question answering datasets demonstrated that our proposed model achieved improved outcomes compared to conventional approaches.

We develop a novel method for creating high dimensional expanders by taking cover graphs of smaller ones. This underlying graph cover can be seen as a higher dimensional geometric construction, which discovers new high dimensional expanders from existing ones. Utilizing this framework, we demonstrate the existence of constant degree high dimensional expanders in any dimension four or higher. Furthermore, we establish a connection between graph cover constructions and invariance of homology in high dimensional expanders, which might be of independent mathematical value.

Recent advancements in language models have enabled them to complete various tasks beyond language generation, but providing relevant task instructions in natural language has proven to be a challenge. Researchers have made progress on generating task instructions, known as prompts, but it becomes increasingly difficult to determine which prompts are effective when presented with multiple options, raising important questions for the future. In this paper, we explore the potential answers to this query by evaluating the performance of different prompts across a range of tasks, including two classification tasks and one ranking task, conducted outside of a formal task setting. The tasks used data from real-world products, requiring models to choose between options provided by the company or user comments, making the selection a more complex process. We discovered that using prompts generated through search or language models performs well but is inferior to using expert-crafted prompts, with improvements seen in models that can interpret task prompts more effectively. However, the lack of consistent performance in models that can interpret tasks, known as reasoning models, makes it challenging to determine which prompt is most effective, highlighting the need for further investigation into the properties of successful prompts.

This study utilizes the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant concept to explore secondary $p$-modular properties of elliptic curves, specifically artinian height spectra and artinian growth rates, in order to establish connections between these properties and the curve's $j$-invariant properties. Research indicates that primary artinian growth rates are directly related to the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant, while exceptional artinian growth rates can be inferred from the curve's $j$-invariant value. Certain boundary values of artinian growth rates can be described by a specific polynomial equation involving the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant. This artinian growth rate function is continuous but not differentiable in the primary range. This work has also provided upper limits for secondary $p$-modular growth rates in elliptic curves.

We have developed an innovative method to detect not just one, but multiple frequencies in microwave fields using Rydberg atoms. This method leverages Rydberg dimers, which respond differently to various microwave frequencies. By employing Rydberg dimer states with unique properties, we can enhance our ability to detect specific frequencies in complex microwave environments. A deep learning technique further enhances our detection capabilities, making them even more sensitive. Our findings expand the scope for using Rydberg atoms in quantum sensing applications and discover new opportunities for quantum information systems.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally bright spiral galaxy, features a prominent central disk that maintains its narrow shape even at very large distances from the galaxy's center. This unusual structure is remarkably similar to that of another galaxy, NGC 691, and consists of a compact core surrounded by a ring of high surface brightness. Despite their notable characteristics, the structures of UGC 8839's outer regions are more typical of spiral galaxies in general, featuring a relatively low surface brightness disk with spiral arms composed of stars and gas.
